p2-4-high-throughput-pretreatment-amp-hydrolysis-a-hcpfb2vjp > 11 Weighing biomass:

Using a spatula, scoop out 75 mg of plant biomass on a paper weighing funnel using an analytical balance. Transfer biomass to glass reactor vials and close with a stopper to avoid moisture and dust.

p2-4-high-throughput-pretreatment-amp-hydrolysis-a-hcpfb2vjp > Addition of solvent:

Weigh 425 mg of solvent based on its density, in the fume hood using a pipette, and transfer the solvent into the glass reactor vials. Mix well and place the reactor vials within the high-throughput HTX reactor.

Use the torque screwdriver to fasten the reactor lids.

p2-4-high-throughput-pretreatment-amp-hydrolysis-a-hcpfb2vjp > Pretreatment set up:

Place the HTX reactor within a secondary container, and place the set up in a hot air oven already preheated and set to 140 C for 3 hours for the pretreatment reaction to occur. Post-pretreatment, cool the set-up down at room temperature and unscrew the reactor vials to set up enzymatic hydrolysis reaction.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

p2-4-high-throughput-pretreatment-amp-hydrolysis-a-hcpfb2vjp > Enzymatic hydrolysis

- 12 Measure the pH of the biomass after pretreatment and adjust it to a range of 4.8 5.2 using 1 Mass Percent citrate buffer, pH 5.0.

p2-4-high-throughput-pretreatment-amp-hydrolysis-a-hcpfb2vjp > Note

Note: When using 0.100 g of biomass (15% solids loading) and 10% cholinium lysinate, approximately 380 µL of buffer is required, depending on the initial pH.

- 13 Prepare a mixture of CTec3:HTec3 enzymatic cocktails at a 9:1 volume ratio. Add the mixture to the pretreated biomass in each vial at a final ratio of 10 mg of enzyme per g of biomass.

1000 µL of enzyme mix contains 104 mg of enzyme. In this protocol, 20 µL of enzyme mix was used.

- 14 Incubate the plate at 50 °C for 72:00:00 . 8°

p2-4-high-throughput-pretreatment-amp-hydrolysis-a-hcpfb2vjp > 15 Finish this section

Post saccharification, the solids are allowed to settle down. The tray with the glass vials is then centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min to separate the solid and liquid parts.

p2-4-high-throughput-pretreatment-amp-hydrolysis-a-hcpfb2vjp > 16 Filter the samples:

Centrifuge the plates in a benchtop plate centrifuge at 4000 rpm for 10 min to precipitate the solid fraction from the aqueous hydrolysate. Transfer 50 µL of hydrolysate from each vial to a 96-well 0.45 µm filter plate using a liquid handler or multichannel pipette. Place the filter plate on top of a collection plate and spin the plate in a benchtop centrifuge at 4000 rpm for 10 min.

- 17 Dilute the samples: Prepare samples for HPLC by diluting the filtered hydrolysates 20 times with water (10 µL sample + 190 µL water) in a Bio-Rad hard shell 96-well plate (Cat # HSP9601). Samples can also be stored at -20 °C until analysis.

-

<!-- image -->

- 18 Analyze the samples in an Agilent Inifinity 1260 HPLC equipped with an Aminex HPX87H column, using 4 mM sulfuric acid as mobile phase, 0.6 mL/min flow rate, 60 ºC column temperature, 20 min run time and a refractive index detector kept at 35 ºC during analysis. Integrate the peak areas and compare to calibration curves made with pure glucose and xylose standards.

It is my pleasure to present the 2024 Agricultural Report for Stanislaus County, pursuant to Sections 2272 and 2279 of the California Food and Agricultural Code. As required by law, this report provides information on the condition of the agricultural industry, including production, value, and the presence of  pests  or  quarantines  within  the  county.  Reported  values  represent  estimated  gross  farm-gate values and do not account for production costs; they should not be interpreted as profit or loss. Local re-spending and support multipliers are not included in these figures.

In 2024, Stanislaus County's total gross value of agricultural production was $3,150,321,000, a 6% decrease from 2023. Almonds experienced a modest increase in value to $824 million, maintaining their position as the county's highest-valued commodity. Milk and poultry remained in second and third place, with slightly lower values of $755 million and $292 million, respectively. Together, these three commodities form the backbone of local agriculture, representing nearly 60% of the county's total agricultural value.

Dairy holds prominence in this years' report for its historical and economic significance to our county, and the extraordinary ways dairy farmers have embraced technology. However, both the poultry and dairy sectors faced significant challenges in 2024 due to Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza. This disease has wreaked havoc in commercial poultry across the United States since 2022, particularly turkey and egg-laying operations locally. In 2024, the virus jumped species, infecting dairy cattle for the first time. In Stanislaus County, the outbreak caused milk production losses in the final quarter and led to the quarantine of more than 80% of the county's dairies.

In addition, 2024 marked the first detection of the Glassy-winged Sharpshooter in Stanislaus County, prompting the implementation of a quarantine and the use of integrated pest management strategies. Our department continues to take a multi-faceted approach to eliminate this invasive pest from our county and protect local agriculture.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > DAIRY IN STANISLAUS COUNTY

We can  thank  immigrants  and  irrigation  for the longstanding history of dairy in our county. After local irrigation districts were formed and water  became  available  near  the  turn  of  the last  century,  farmers  gravitated  towards  high value crops like alfalfa. This ideal feed for cattle allowed cows to be kept closer to milking barns, rather than on open range.

Early immigrants familiar to European dairying began to shape the industry. Small family dairies with a few dozen milking cows supplying nearby communities were a common sight in the area. Many local dairies still  bear  Portuguese,  Swiss, and Dutch names.

California's unique, isolated position bordered by  the  mountains,  desert  and  sea  made  it  an island market. Advances  and  efficiencies  in technology such as pasteurization, refrigeration, and transportation allowed creameries and cooperatives to process safer milk with longer shelf life for shipment to metropolitan areas in the state.

By 1909,  73%  of  land  irrigated  by  Modesto Irrigation District was planted to alfalfa for cattle feed. The dairy industry had doubled between 1904  and  1909,  surpassing  the  longstanding dominance  of  wheat  production. The  local Milk Producers Association grew to one of the nations' largest dairy cooperatives. By the mid 20 th  century, Stanislaus County became one of the top producing dairy counties in the nation. It even hosted a weekly dairy radio show, which played a key role in the passage of the California Milk Pooling Act in 1969 - legislation modeled after the Federal Milk Marketing Orders.

Far from the hand milked 30 cow dairies and home-marketed dairy products of the past, the average California dairy today is around 1,000 head, some of the nation's largest. Yet, nearly all are still exclusively family owned.

Nutritionists are employed to optimize diets - even to the specific individual cow's production. A typical Holstein - the most common breed of dairy cow - now produces over 10 gallons of milk per day thanks to diet and genetic selection. In  fact,  according  to  the  National  Ag  Statistics Service, milk production per cow has increased 8.1% over just the last 10 years!

Photo: Cadence Egli at her family dairy

<!-- image -->

Technology continues to advance dairy production  to  levels  unfathomable  at  the  turn of the 20 th century. Artificial insemination increases  premier  genetic  availability  and  is safer  for  farmers  and  cows.  Sexed  semen facilitates marketing animals to meet both dairy replacement  heifer  and  even  beef  demand. Barns are designed for optimal cow comfort with fans,  misters,  free  stalls,  and  various  bedding materials - some even have water beds! Cows are milked more efficiently and even robotically in  some  cases.  Milk  barn  designs  are  more ergonomic  for  workers,  reducing  the  need  to squat or bend.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > DAIRY IN STANISLAUS COUNTY

Artificial insemination increases  premier  genetic  availability  and  is safer  for  farmers  and  cows. Sexed  semen facilitates marketing animals to meet both dairy replacement  heifer  and  even  beef  demand. Barns are designed for optimal cow comfort with fans,  misters,  free  stalls,  and  various  bedding materials - some even have water beds! Cows are milked more efficiently and even robotically in  some  cases. Milk  barn  designs  are  more ergonomic  for  workers,  reducing  the  need  to squat or bend.

Being  the  leader  in  dairy  production  comes with environmental responsibility. Municipal and food manufacturing wastes are being diverted from landfills to feed cattle. Scientists and  dieticians  are  experimenting  with  feed combinations  that  create  less  methane  in  the cow's  digestive  system.  Manure  methane  is also  being  captured  and  utilized  for  power production.

Stanislaus County's 132 dairies produce nearly 12% of the milk in the state, putting the county third highest in production. Local modern dairies continue  to  set  the  pace  in  advances  in  milk production and serve a major role of importance to our county's economy.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > DAIRY INSPECTIONS

<!-- image -->

As one of California's leading dairyproducing regions, public health standards and consumer confidence is maintained by rigorous inspection  by  Stanislaus  County  Department of Environmental Resources' two Milk and Dairy Inspectors. Stanislaus is one of only eight counties with a California Department of Agriculture Approved Milk Inspection Service.

Milk on-farm is sampled for bacteria levels and antibiotic residues, and farm sanitation practices are observed. Milk production and handling must comply  with  California  Food  and  Agricultural Code, California  Code  of  Regulations,  and  the current edition of the US Public Health Service Pasteurized Milk Ordinance. Inspectors also assist with best  practices for facilities  and equipment, investigations, permitting, and other special projects.

Photos: Ryan Barney, Stanislaus Dept. Environmental Resources

<!-- image -->

The  importance  of our sister agency in maintaining  compliance  with  established  rules and regulations upholds the safety, quality, and integrity of milk produced within the County.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza in Dairies: A New Challenge

Since 2022, Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (H5N1) has decimated commercial poultry flocks across the country, including in Stanislaus County. In 2024, the disease crossed species into dairy herds out of state. The first occurrence of H5N1 in Central Valley dairy cows was reported in late August and Stanislaus confirmed an initial case in early September.

In response to the new viral threat, dairies increased biosecurity and quarantine measures and provided  personal  protective  equipment  to  employees.  Disinfection  stations,  new  or  infected

animal isolation and frequent cleaning of water troughs and other shared spaces became routine.

Despite  these  precautions,  the  virus  spread  rapidly among  high-density  cow  populations,  leading  to  the quarantine  of  more  than  110  dairies  -  over  80%  of the  dairy  production  in  Stanislaus  County  between November 2024 and April 2025. In December, a statewide  emergency  was  declared  to  expedite  preparedness and cross-agency response. Unlike poultry, infections in cattle did not result in high mortality, but notable losses in milk production occurred over the last quarter of the year and into 2025.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > INTRODUCTION:

California is a leading agricultural state, producing over 400 commodities, many of which generate byproducts that can be used as feed for dairy cattle. Stanislaus County, with strong almond and dairy industries,  is  an  example  of  this  integration:  almond  hulls,  a  byproduct  of  almond  processing,  are routinely fed to dairy cows. Byproducts have become an essential part of dairy rations, offering costeffective feed solutions while enhancing the State's sustainability practices. However, little research has been done to quantify the extent of byproduct use in California dairy farms. Given the increasing regulations on water usage, byproducts may play an even more critical role in feeding dairy cattle in the coming years. This survey aimed to identify commonly used byproducts, estimate the proportion of dairy rations made up of byproducts, and assess trends in their usage.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > SURVEY RESPONDENTS:

In March 2022, an electronic survey was sent to 61 nutritionists across the state. We received 26  returned  surveys  (46%  response  rate).  Respondents  provided  services  to  498  dairy  farms, representing approximately 936,700 milking cows. These farms accounted for 44.5% of all California dairies, providing a comprehensive assessment of byproduct usage in dairy rations. Most herds were in the San Joaquin Valley (87.6%), with smaller numbers in Northern California (5.5%) and Southern California (6.9%).

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > COMMONLY USED BYPRODUCTS:

A total of 58 byproducts were reported as being used in dairy rations; the most commonly utilized are described in Table 1.

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Almond hulls were the most frequently cited byproduct used as a forage replacement in lactating cow rations, reported by 88.5% of responding nutritionists. When used as concentrate replacements, citrus byproducts (30.8%) were the most frequently mentioned. A 2012 survey of California dairy farms found that almond hulls were included in lactating cow diets at an average of three pounds per cow per day. A more recent survey (conducted in 2022) reported increased almond hull utilization, averaging five pounds per cow per day. As California produces nearly 80% of the world's almonds, an abundant supply of almond hulls is available for dairy rations. Their moderate neutral detergent fiber (NDF) content and highly fermentable carbohydrates make them suitable as replacements for both forages and concentrates. Similarly, California accounts for 79% of total U.S. citrus production, ensuring a steady supply of citrus byproducts. Rich in pectin and sugars, citrus byproducts serve as substitute for traditional high-energy concentrates.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > BYPRODUCT INCLUSION RATES IN DAIRY RATIONS:

In this study, the weighted, average byproduct inclusion rate in California lactating cow rations was estimated at 40.9% on a dry matter (DM) basis. This estimate was calculated by weighting nutritionists' reported average DM byproduct inclusion rates with the number of lactating cows they served. For comparison, 2021 work estimated a national average of 32% inclusion for lactating dairy diets. The higher byproduct inclusion rates observed in California likely reflect the state's abundant supply of agricultural byproducts.

The inclusion rate of byproducts in dairy rations varied widely as follows:

- LACTATING COWS: 10-80% (average: 39.8%, not weighted by cow numbers)
- DRY COWS: 5-80% (average: 35.4%)
- HEIFERS: 5-80% (average: 36.0%)

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > TRENDS IN BYPRODUCT USAGE:

Over the previous five years, most nutritionists (68%) reported an increase in byproduct usage. A smaller proportion reported decreased (12%) or unchanged (20%) usage. Looking ahead, 80% of nutritionists anticipate further increases in byproduct use, while 12% predict a decrease and 8% foresee no change.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > IMPLICATIONS FOR DAIRY INDUSTRY:

The extensive use of byproducts in California dairy rations provides numerous benefits

- COST-EFFECTIVE: Byproducts offer an economical alternative to traditional feed ingredients.
- FLEXIBILITY IN DIET FORMULATION: Nutritionists can adjust rations based on the availability and price of products.
- SUSTAINABILITY: Feeding byproducts reduces landfill waste and water consumption.
- DEMONSTRATING SUSTAINABILITY TO CONSUMERS AND LEGISLATORS: As environmental concerns and regulatory pressures increase, it is essential for the dairy industry to highlight its sustainable feeding practices. By incorporating byproducts, dairies contribute to a circular economy, repurposing agricultural residues into valuable feed sources. Effectively communicating these efforts to consumers and policymakers can strengthen support for the industry.

10 EGGS, ALL > 6 > CONCLUSIONS:

The results of this survey confirm that byproducts are a key component of California dairy rations, with an average inclusion rate of 40.9%. The large range of byproduct feeding rates for lactating rations (0-80% DM) may indicate an opportunity to increase byproduct inclusion rates in California dairy rations on some farms. Overall, the consumption of byproducts benefits not only the dairy industry, but those industries that produce the byproducts.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Regional Overview & Strategic Context

The North San Joaquin Valley-comprising San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced Counties-generates approximately 3.2 to 4.6 million tons of agricultural byproducts and woody biomass annually across the residue streams evaluated in this report. Most of this material is already committed to established livestock-feed, soil-management, energy, or industrial markets. The fraction realistically available to new projects is smaller and highly dependent on feedstock ownership, seasonality, moisture content, existing contracts, and transportation distance.

The region's byproduct economy is nevertheless undergoing a significant transition. Agricultural burn restrictions have shifted woody biomass toward active management, declining biomass-power demand is creating pressure on established shell and wood outlets, and water-quality and operational requirements increasingly influence the management of wet processing residuals. At the same time, biochar, stabilized food and feed ingredients, and selected extractive markets offer opportunities for higher-value utilization where projects can be co-located with concentrated feedstock sources and integrated with existing processing infrastructure.

This transition is driven by three factors:

1. Strict Policy Mandates : The final implementation of California Senate Bill 705 and San Joaquin Valley Air Pollution Control District (SJVAPCD) Rule 4103 has effectively eliminated open agricultural burning as of January 1, 2025, forcing massive volumes of woody biomass into actively managed handling pathways.
2. Economic & Environmental Volatility : Fluctuating livestock feed prices, dairy herd consolidation, and stringent regional water quality restrictions (CVRWQCB Waste Discharge Requirements) are destabilizing traditional cost-avoidance outlets.

3. Emerging High-Value Markets : Regulatory milestones (such as FDA GRAS status for almond hull powder in May 2026), expanding biochar incentive frameworks, and premium pet food demand are creating selective high-value upcycling opportunities for stabilized residuals.

This report provides a comprehensive cross-commodity baseline of byproduct availability, economic drivers, logistical constraints, and emerging valorization opportunities to guide project developers, processors, and regional stakeholders.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > A. Dry, Lignocellulosic Residues (Almond Shells, Walnut Shells, Woody Biomass)

- Logistical Dominance & Transport Ceilings : These dry materials possess excellent storage stability (>1 year). However, their low bulk density creates volumetric freight bottlenecks. For low-value, undensified materials, transportation economics generally deteriorate rapidly beyond approximately 20-40 miles. Higher-value products, favorable backhauls, or densification can support longer movements.
- The Biomass Power Pivot to Biochar : Traditional biomass cogeneration facilities are rapidly closing across California, eliminating a historical bulk relief valve. Pyrolysis and biochar production are emerging as potential replacement outlets, supported by federal cost-shares (USDA NRCS Practice 336: $760-$930/acre), state grants (CDFA Healthy Soils: up to $200,000), and private carbon removal credits (Puro.earth: $125-$180/ton CO₂).
- Industrial Value Spreads : Walnut shells illustrate a major secondary processing spread. While raw, unsifted shells straight from the cracker trade at $30-$70/ton, secondary aggregators clean, mill, and size the dense shell fraction into precision abrasive blasting and filtration media  that can sell as a processed industrial product for approximately $900 to $1,400 per ton .

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > B. High-Moisture Residuals (Grape, Tomato, and Olive Pomace; Walnut Hulls)

- Extreme Perishability Bottlenecks : High moisture content (55-80%) triggers rapid biological degradation, fermentation, and mold. White wine pomace spoils in 12-24 hours, red pomace in 24-72 hours, and wet tomato pomace ferments within days. Certain high-value bioactive fractions begin degrading within hours of processing, requiring rapid separation, cooling, stabilization, or extraction. The applicable processing window is feedstock- and compound-specific.
- Compliance Liabilities vs. Premium Value Split : Processors view wet streams as operational risks that threaten plant shutdowns or water quality permit violations (CVRWQCB Waste Discharge Requirements).
- The Tomato Example : Wet tomato pomace sells locally to cattle dairies for $45-$75/ton wet. However, the 15% of pomace that is mechanically dried commands $500 to $700 per ton in the premium pet food market.

- The Walnut Hull Exception : Walnut hulls contain juglone, a compound toxic to horses and unpalatable to cattle, excluding them from livestock feed and forcing 75-85% of hulls into zero-value land application.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > C. Established Commodity Co-Products (Almond Hulls)

- Dairy Integration & Pricing Volatility : Almond hulls represent a mature, sugar-rich feed commodity representing over 1.1 million tons statewide. More than 90% enters livestock-feed markets, primarily serving California dairy operations . However, prices are highly volatile, peaking at $217/ton during the 2022 drought before dropping to $74/ton in 2024.
- Regulatory Catalysts : The FDA's designation of almond hull powder as Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) in May 2026 establishes a regulatory pathway to upcycle hulls into human food fiber and nutraceuticals, unlocking 5x to 15x value multipliers.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Key Policy, Infrastructure, & Market Drivers

1. Agricultural Burn Restrictions (SB 705 & SJVAPCD Rule 4103) : Open burning prohibitions enforced as of 2025 have driven widespread adoption of Whole Orchard Recycling (WOR), which now accounts for 60-75% of almond removal acreage. Public incentives-including payments of up to $600/acre through SJVAPCD and $862/acre through eligible CDFA practices, can enable WOR to approach cost parity with historical burning, subject to program eligibility and restrictions on duplicative funding.
2. Structural Crop Disparities in Incentives : Incentive programs pay on a per-acre basis, creating economic inequities across crop types. Walnut removals generate 80-120 tons of dense biomass per acre compared to 30-65 tons per acre for almonds, leaving walnut growers with a significantly lower subsidy per ton to cover higher grinding costs.
3. Industry & Infrastructure Concentratio n: Processing capacity across the NSJV is heavily concentrated:
- Grapes: Large conglomerates control 75-80% of regional pomace, with third-party haulers like G3 Enterprises handling >40% of California's total pomace volume.
- Tomatoes: The Morning Star Packing Company leverages industrial triple-pass drum dryers, solar fields, and bulk rail line logistics to dominate the $500-$700/ton pet food market, leaving smaller independent canners tied to local wet feed markets.
4. Municipal & Industrial Closed-Loop Innovation :

- Modesto's Segregated Cannery Sewer: Modesto operates a dedicated, segregated sewer line during summer canning season to route millions of gallons of high-solids fruit/vegetable processing wastewater to dedicated settling basins.
- Musco Family Olive Co. CHP Engine: Musco combusts on-site olive pits in specialized boilers to distill high-salinity process wastewater, powering a steam engine that generates approximately 500 kW (supplying ~50% of the facility's electricity needs).

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Strategic Recommendations for Project Developers & Processors

- Prioritize Co-Location & Distributed Infrastructure : Because transportation economics deteriorate rapidly for low-value, high-moisture, or low-density materials, conversion technologies generally favor co-location or near-site deployment at centralized huller/shellers, canneries, or large mills rather than standalone regional hubs.
- Capitalize on Incentive Stacking & Carbon Finance : Evaluate complementary, non-duplicative incentives across biomass collection, conversion, biochar application, soil-health practices, and carbon crediting. Eligibility, additionality, and restrictions on funding the same activity must be evaluated project by project.
- Solve the Moisture/Perishability Barrier : High-value extraction pathways may require separation, cooling, stabilization, or low-energy drying within hours of processing, depending on the feedstock and target compound.
- Leverage Regulatory Exemption Thresholds : Small wineries and custom-crush facilities should evaluate whether their self-generated pomace composting operations qualify for the higher SB 279 exemption threshold, while separately addressing applicable water-quality, air-quality, nuisance, and site-management requirements.
- Consider Designing for Seasonal Peak Capacity : Facilities should be sized based on peak daily generation and the duration of the processing season, not annual tonnage alone. Projects should identify storage, off-season utilization, or modular operating strategies before advancing to development.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Summary

Almond byproducts are abundant and have been widely valued as a commodity for decades throughout the NSJV. Animal feed is the overwhelming pathway for hulls, while pathways that favor ease of logistics dominate the usage of shells. There have been significant investments by the industry to develop new use cases and markets which can bring significant value to the almond supply chain.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Supply and Characteristics

By acreage, almonds are the single largest crop across all three counties in the North San Joaquin Valley, comprising more than 500,000 acres and contributing more than $1.7B in economic value to the region from the kernel (or nut meat) alone. On a field-weight basis, a typical harvest load is roughly 50% hull, 25-30% kernel, and 20-25% shell (excluding orchard debris which will be discussed in a later chapter). This whole fruit, referred to as a drupe, is mechanically shaken from the tree and allowed to dry on the orchard floor before being collected and transported to a processing facility for hulling and shelling.

Figure 1-1. Almond Harvest by anatomical fraction based on county crop report data.

<!-- image -->

The hulling and shelling process is a crucial step that separates these components. First, the bulk material goes through pre-cleaning to remove debris like sticks and rocks. It then passes through a series of shear rolls or cylinders which crack and peel away the hull. The hulled almond (still in its shell) then moves to the shelling stage, where another set of rollers cracks the hard outer shell to release the edible kernel. Vibrating screens and air blowers are used throughout the process to efficiently separate the light hulls and shells from the heavier kernels, with any remaining debris or unseparated nuts recycled back for re-processing to maximize yield.

Each anatomical fraction has a distinct composition and use cases. The almond kernel is the high-value product, rich in fats (around 50%, primarily monounsaturated), protein (around 21%), dietary fiber, and essential nutrients like Vitamin E and magnesium. The hull, which is anatomically similar to the fleshy part of a peach or apricot, is high in extractives, fiber, and phytochemicals. Conversely, the shell is a hard, woody fraction that is much higher in fiber.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Summary of Material Flows and Use Cases

Figure 1-2 and Table 1-1 below illustrate the typical material flows and use cases for almond meats, by-products, and the handling of woody residues (thinnings, prunings, removals) by the almond orchards. Material handling arrangements vary across the valley and from orchard to orchard, but it is common for the almond drupe material to change hands multiple times from the point of harvest through transportation, processing, and end formulation/markets. Hauling arrangements vary-in some cases the orchard will haul themselves (often offset by hauling/trucking allowances as described further below) or will contract out these hauling services.

- Truck transport costs ranging $4-6/mile for a full truck, with 20-24 tons of almond/truck
- 3-year yield averages and price ranges from Merced, San Joaquin, and Stanislaus county crop reports (Merced County, n.d.; San Joaquin County Agricultural Commissioner / Sealer of Weights & Measures, n.d.; Stanislaus County Agricultural Commissioner, n.d)

- 30 (low) to 65 (high) tons/acre for orchard removal (Almond Board of California, n.d.), 0.64-0.96 tons/acre for prunings (Aliaño-González et al., 2022), 19,000 acres of removal/yr (Almond Board of California, 2024)
- Hauling costs typically represent 20-40% of the delivered cost of hulls or shells, depending on distance and seasonal availabilityThere are several important organizational and contractual models underpinning the almond industry, with agricultural cooperatives playing a central role.

Regional service cooperatives, such as the Central California Almond Growers Association, are grower-owned entities formed to provide essential shared services, primarily hulling, shelling, and storage. These co-ops establish member service fees and delivery schedules prior to harvest, and after operating costs and coproduct revenues are accounted for, dividends are distributed back to members based on throughput. All revenues for kernels/meats are allocated back to the almond grower. Industrial/marketing cooperatives, such as Blue Diamond Growers, take the hulling, shelling, and storage services cooperative model further by vertically integrating downstream steps including advanced processing, value-added product formulation into finished consumer goods, marketing, and R&D. Their payment structures are typically more complex, using graded pooling systems and multi-stage returns to growers. Outside of cooperative structures, many independent growers contract directly with private huller/sheller operations. In these arrangements, growers retain revenue from kernel weights while processors typically capture value from hull and shell coproducts. Hauling arrangements vary: some growers transport their own loads, while others rely on third-party agricultural haulers. Cooperatives account for a large portion of almond handling and marketing in the Central Valley, making the co-op model more common than fully independent arrangements, especially among diversified family farms. However, precise estimates of the volumes or percentages handled across these different models are not publicly available.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Almond Hauling/Transportation

Transportation of harvested almond drupes from orchards to huller/sheller facilities represents a small but important component of overall harvest costs, and the economics are shaped heavily by cooperative hauling agreements. In California's almond industry, most growers rely on short-haul trucking-typically end-dump or live-bottom Key Economic Insight: The 20-Mile Hauling Radius > Transporting almond drupes is generally economical only within 20 miles of a receiving facility. Commercial hauling costs ($4-$6 per loaded truck-mile) combined with cooperative per-ton allowances cap grower reimbursement, making proximity critical to profitability.

trailers-to move in-hull almonds from the field to a nearby huller/sheller. Almond drupe transportation costs-from the orchard to the huller/sheller-are typically reported using per-ton delivery allowances. Cooperative processors such as Blue Diamond Growers publish trucking allowances that compensate growers or contracted haulers based on the distance hauled, with recent schedules showing rates such as $11.00 per ton for approximately 0.6-15 miles and $12.60 per ton for 15+ miles (Bluediamondgrowers.com, 2025). These rates effectively cap grower hauling expenses and provide a predictable reimbursement structure. These trucking allowances are designed as a cost-share mechanism for growers-not a market-rate reimbursement. In contrast, UC-Davis cost and return studies embed 'haul to huller/sheller' within broader harvest operations, combining sweeping, pickup, hauling, hulling, and shelling into a single per-acre cost without isolating transportation as a standalone line item (Duncan et al., 2024). As a result, modeling transportation economics requires explicit assumptions about yield (tons per acre), haul distance, and whether the grower receives cooperative trucking allowances or pays an independent hauler directly. These per-ton delivery allowances significantly influence real-world cost structures and determine how far orchards can economically be located from their nearest huller/sheller. transportation is typically economical only when the orchard is within 20 miles of the receiving facility,

Regardless of whether a grower is a member of a cooperative or not, these hauling costs indicate that assuming an average delivered yield of 2.5 tons of dry kernel per acre. At typical commercial hauling rates of $4-6 per loaded truck-mile (or around $0.17-0.30 per ton-mile when a truck carries 20-24 tons of drupes), per-acre hauling expenditures remain modest. However, these figures assume efficient truck turnaround, minimal wait times at the huller/sheller, full payloads, and cooperative or contract pricing rather than spot hauling. Because huller/shellers have limited geographic service areas and strong economies of scale, most growers select facilities within short distances, which keeps per-acre transportation costs predictable and low relative to other operational costs.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Hull Production and Supply

Hulls are the fleshy, carbohydrate- and fiber-rich layer that surrounds the almond shell and kernel. Almond hull production in counties such as San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced can be reliably estimated using the publicly available county agricultural commissioner reports, which document bearing acreage, yields, and nut-meat output. By applying standard hull-to-kernel conversion factors, these data provide robust estimates of total hull volume generated annually in the region.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Hull Utilization and Market Structure

Efficient and consistent utilization of almond hulls is central to their value. However, utilization cannot be precisely measured at a county or regional level because California's primary public dataset on feed use - the California Department of Food and Agriculture (CDFA) Commercial Feed Tonnage Report - publishes only statewide totals for almond-hull tonnage; it does not track origin, destination, or county-level flows. As a result, assessing local hull demand and matching supply to feed use requires inference based on industry structure rather than direct measurement. Nevertheless, well-documented patterns indicate that almond hulls remain a major feed commodity. For decades, dairy nutritionists in California have incorporated almond hulls into cattle feed rations as a cost-effective partial substitute for alfalfa and other fibrous feedstuffs. This relationship has contributed to the mutual economic viability of the almond and dairy sectors, which are geographically co-located throughout the region. CDFA reports show more than 1.1 million tons of almond hulls annually entering commercial feed channels (California Department of Food and Agriculture, 2024). Industry sources-including processors, cooperatives, and agricultural outreach - commonly report that 90-97% of marketed hulls are used in livestock feed, primarily by dairies (Somerville et al., 2020). Given the high density of dairy operations in Merced and Stanislaus Counties and processing capacity in San Joaquin County, the NSJV functions effectively as a major hull-supply zone with co-located demand. Inter-county movement of hulls is widely understood to be routine. Processors in counties with high almond-hulling capacity often ship hulls to neighboring counties with dairy-focused feed demand. Some hulls are even shipped out of state. Consequently, hull production in one county does not necessarily correspond to local hull consumption. Instead, the linkage between almond processing and dairy feed demand ensures that hulls generated in the NSJV are overwhelmingly directed toward livestock feed markets. Therefore, while county-level feed utilization data are lacking, the combined geography of almond processing infrastructure and dairy operations strongly suggests that virtually all hulls produced in the NSJV enter livestock feed channels, either locally or through inter-county transport. The NSJV therefore operates as a cohesive almond-hull supply-and-demand hub.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Hull Pricing Dynamics and Market Drivers

Almond hulls are a traded feed commodity, and their price fluctuates in response to supply-and-demand dynamics, competing feed sources, and broader market conditions. Hulls and shells are handled by huller/sheller operations and represent a major fraction of the operating revenue of these entities- in 2024 the Central California Almond Growers Association reported that more than 80% of their revenue was derived from hull and shell sales (Central California Almond Growers Association, 2024). While that number may reflect a specific co-op case, it illustrates the central role of byproducts in the processor revenue model. At the county level, annual weighted-average processor-to-gate prices have been recorded in County Crop Reports for Merced, San Joaquin, and Stanislaus Counties, providing decades of historical data on hull price and volume. The sharp rise in hull prices in 2022-briefly exceeding $200 per ton-was driven by drought conditions and substantial reductions in the availability of alternative forage and fiber feedstuffs, including alfalfa hay, straw, and corn silage (see figure 1-4 above). Between 2017 and 2023, corn silage production in the three-county region declined by approximately 780,000 tons (10%), while alfalfa production declined by about 266,000 tons (30%). These reductions in forage availability placed upward pressure on feed prices generally, contributing to increased demand for hulls even as herd sizes remained relatively stable. Because almond hulls serve as a partial substitute for other fibrous feed ingredients, their price and utilization are strongly influenced by the availability and cost of alfalfa hay, straw, silage, and other byproducts. Hulls become more cost-competitive when forage production falls or input prices for alternative feeds rise.

In 2023, hull prices declined sharply as larger carryover inventories from the previous crop year became available and feed markets adjusted. Prices returned to a range of approximately $80-$125 per ton, more consistent with historical norms for the region.

Future utilization and pricing of almond hulls will depend not only on annual almond production but also on the long-term trajectory of the region's dairy sector, which has shown gradual consolidation and modest geographic shifts in herd distribution. This creates motivation for hullers/shellers to create additional markets, given the significant revenues derived from these byproducts. Seasonal moisture conditions and limited drying capacity can result in variable storage volumes ('carry-over') between crop years, contributing to year-to-year swings in hull availability and price.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Alternative and Emerging Uses: Soil Amendment and Bioenergy

Alternative pathways-such as composting, soil amendment, landfill disposal, or energy generation-account for only a small share of total hull tonnage statewide, and there is scant evidence that these alternatives play major roles in Merced, Stanislaus, or San Joaquin Counties. In fact, some of the compositional attributes of the hulls themselves can be problematic for uses like composting due to high carbohydrate content that can disrupt the microbial consortia (Hartman et al., 2024). Emerging use cases for almond hulls center on upcycling this abundant byproduct into higher-value food, ingredient, and biomaterial applications. Food scientists have identified hulls as a rich source of dietary fiber, polyphenols, natural sugars, and antioxidants, making them promising candidates for incorporation into human food products (Almond Board of California, 2025). Early research has evaluated almond-hull powders as a partial flour substitute in baked goods, increasing fiber and antioxidant content while maintaining acceptable sensory qualities at modest inclusion rates. Pilot projects supported by the Almond Board of California have also explored hull-derived ingredients for nutrition bars, beverages with coffee- or tea-like profiles, and functional food additives leveraging antioxidant or antimicrobial properties (Fusaro, 2023). In May 2026, almond hull powder was designated by FDA as  Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS). GRAS status will create a pathway for high value upcycled food ingredients to access a variety of markets (Almond Board of California, 2026). Importantly, allergen designation will still be a hurdle and limit some market access. Beyond food, almond hulls are being investigated for use in bioproducts, bio-extraction, and sustainable materials (Cao et al., 2025). Their high carbohydrate and polyphenol content make them suitable feedstocks for fermentation, yielding products such as organic acids, ethanol, and specialty chemicals. Researchers are also extracting tannins, pigments, and antioxidant compounds for use in cosmetics, nutraceuticals, and natural preservatives (Najari et al., 2022). While market sizes for these high end applications are very small, unit prices can exceed $10,000/ton at high purity. In the materials space, hulls are being tested in bioplastics, biodegradable composites, and biochar for soil enhancement or carbon sequestration. As the almond industry seeks avenues to increase sustainability and reduce reliance on livestock feed markets, these emerging use cases position hulls as a versatile raw material for multiple circular-economy pathways. It is important to note that while the unit prices are much higher for these applications, final product yields (mass of product per mass of feedstock) are low: typically less than 1 wt%.

Industry-wide data compiled by the Almond Board of California indicate that roughly 70% of almond shells are used for animal bedding; the remaining shells are distributed among soil amendment, limited dairy-feed applications, and energy production (e.g., bioenergy) (Lewis et al., 2020). This allocation highlights the relatively modest-but still important-markets beyond bedding.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Shell Pricing, Logistics, and Market Constraints

Because bedding remains the dominant end use, almond shells function as a low-cost, locally traded commodity. For most huller/shellers, selling shells to the same entity that purchases their hulls is the most operationally efficient and cost-effective option, as it consolidates transportation logistics, minimizes load turnaround times, and reduces the complexity of coordinating multiple outbound markets. Further, due to their low bulk density, shells require substantial storage space, which limits the ability of many processors to stockpile material and reinforces the need for consistent, nearby outlets.

The shells' high lignin and fiber content makes them durable, relatively resistant to decomposition, and gives them some natural absorbency suitable for managing moisture and odor in livestock pens. Price trends are shown in Figure 1-6 (below). Their market value is primarily influenced by:

- Shell quality-driven largely by moisture content, particle size, and the degree of hull-fine or soil contamination (assessed by huller/shellers),
- dairy herd size and bedding demand,
- availability and cost of alternative bedding materials (e.g., sawdust, wood shavings, rice hulls),
- hauling distances between processors and dairy operations, and
- overall almond production volumes.

Figure 1-6. Annual almond shell pricing as reported by the Merced, San Joaquin, and Stanislaus County Annual County Crop Reports.

<!-- image -->

Almond shells continue to be widely used for dairy and poultry bedding owing to their availability and cost-effectiveness, but several long-term trends complicate market stability. California's dairy sector has experienced gradual consolidation and, in some regions, herd contraction. At the same time, almond production-and therefore shell output-has expanded significantly over the past two decades. This imbalance has placed downward pressure on shell values, particularly in years of high almond production. Because shells are produced in large volumes relative to regional bedding demand and have limited high-value alternative markets, their price is often supply-driven and subject to downward pressure in high-production years. This can result in oversupply and accumulation of these materials at huller/sheller processing facilities, resulting in carry-over into subsequent years.

content:
Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Alternative and Emerging Uses: Soil Amendment and Bioenerg

Although the majority of shells are still used for bedding, they have additional applications. Almond shells can act as a soil-conditioning amendment when incorporated into agricultural soils, improving aeration and drainage in a manner similar to wood chips or perlite. Their high carbon and potassium content can contribute to soil structure, though their low nitrogen content means they are not substitute for compost. They remain a comparatively low-cost soil amendment: commercial compost typically costs on the order of $20-$60 per cubic yard, whereas almond shells-depending on processing and transport-are often available at lower bulk costs, commonly in the range of roughly $5-$25 per cubic yard near production regions. A modest share of almond shells continues to be used in bioenergy production. In the North San Joaquin Valley, two biomass power facilities remain operational, with a combined capacity of approximately 57.5 MW, consuming roughly 450,000 tons per year of woody biomass and agricultural residues, including nut shells (DTE Stockton LLC, n.d.; Power Technology, 2024). Almond shells are well suited to combustion due to their low moisture content (<10%) and relatively high calorific value (18-19 MJ/kg). They may be screened, ground, or pelletized to improve handling and transport efficiency, though pelletization introduces additional processing costs, creating a tradeoff between densification and transport economics. Statewide, biomass power generation has declined steadily over the past decade as production costs have risen relative to other renewable energy sources-particularly low-cost solar photovoltaics and wind-making biomass facility power-purchase agreements less favorable. Because biomass facilities are typically far more efficient thermally than electrically, their economic viability increasingly depends on capturing beneficial uses of process heat.

Looking ahead, traditional markets for shells are expected to remain relatively stable but limited, while emerging applications-such as engineered biochar, composite materials, and filtration media-are being researched but have yet to scale commercially.

content:
Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Seasonality, Stability, and Storage Constraints of Byproduct Streams

Almond hulls and shells are generated during hulling and shelling immediately following harvest, which in California is highly concentrated between August and November. As a result, the majority of annual hull and shell production occurs within a relatively short processing window, creating a pronounced seasonal surge in byproduct availability. This temporal concentration has important implications for logistics, storage infrastructure, and the feasibility of year-round utilization pathways. Unlike more perishable agricultural residues (particularly high-moisture pomace fractions), hulls and shells possess physicochemical characteristics that make them more amenable to bulk storage and extended use beyond the harvest and processing period.

Figure 1-7. Seasonal dynamics of gross almond hull generation (flow, right axis) and inventory levels (stock, left axis) in the NSJV region.

Harvest-driven production is concentrated between August and November (shaded area), resulting in rapid stockpile accumulation followed by gradual drawdown during the remainder of the year.

Unlike more perishable agricultural residues (particularly high-moisture pomace fractions), hulls and shells possess physicochemical characteristics that make them more amenable to bulk storage and extended use beyond the harvest and processing period. Figure 1-7. Seasonal dynamics of gross almond hull generation (flow, right axis) and inventory levels (stock, left axis) in the NSJV region.

<!-- image -->

Harvest-driven production is concentrated between August and November (shaded area), resulting in rapid stockpile accumulation followed by gradual drawdown during the remainder of the year.

Inventory is typically reduced prior to the subsequent harvest cycle to maintain storage capacity and manage seasonal supply fluctuations 2 . Almond hulls contain higher levels of soluble carbohydrates, including mono- and oligosaccharides, and have moderately higher moisture content compared to the shell fraction. Nevertheless, hulls are sufficiently stable to allow for bulk storage, commonly in large outdoor piles at processing sites or feed yards. Key storage considerations include minimizing moisture (e.g., use of tarps or covered storage) and ensuring adequate aeration to reduce microbial activity, dry matter losses, and the risk of spontaneous heating. For traditional uses such as animal feed, hulls can be stored for months with limited loss of nutritive value when handled appropriately so long as they continue to meet quality standards of moisture, ash, and fiber content (DePeters et al., 2020). Their storability underpins their role as a year-round feed ingredient, despite their highly seasonal production. Beyond material stability, storage duration is also shaped by inventory turnover and space constraints, as processors and feedlots generally aim to clear or reduce stockpiles before the next harvest season to accommodate the annual surge in byproduct generation.  Hulling and shelling operations are particularly sensitive to carryover volumes, as excess inventory can contribute to regional oversupply and price volatility, as observed in recent market cycles (e.g., 2022-2023). For emerging valorization pathways, particularly those targeting fermentable sugars or other bio-based chemical precursors, storage duration and conditions become more consequential. Extended storage may result in partial degradation of soluble sugars through microbial metabolism or leaching under wet conditions, potentially affecting conversion efficiency and product yields. Under silo or silage-like conditions, almond hulls undergo measurable fermentative and microbial transformations, shifting pH and organic composition during storage (Sırakaya, 2023). For higher-value applications such as human dietary fiber ingredients, storage requirements are substantially more stringent than for feed or bulk material uses. In these contexts, almond hulls must meet food-grade standards for microbial load, mycotoxins, chemical residues, and physical contaminants. Extended outdoor stockpiling, while acceptable for feed or bioenergy uses, can introduce variability in moisture, microbial load, or environmental contaminants, complicating downstream purification and regulatory compliance. In these contexts, almond hulls must meet food-grade standards for microbial load, mycotoxins, chemical residues, and physical contaminants. Extended outdoor stockpiling, while acceptable for feed or bioenergy uses, can introduce variability in moisture, microbial load, or environmental contaminants, complicating downstream purification and regulatory compliance. As a result, material destined for human consumption may require segregation at the processor, controlled storage conditions (e.g., covered or

2

Note data reflected is modeled data based on 2024 almond hull production and storage enclosed facilities), and tighter monitoring of moisture and temperature (Almond Board of California, 2025). Additionally, preservation of functional properties becomes critical. For fiber ingredients, characteristics such as soluble versus insoluble fiber composition, particle size, water-holding capacity, and fermentability influence product performance and labeling claims. Prolonged storage under fluctuating humidity conditions may alter these properties through partial carbohydrate degradation or physicochemical changes in the cell wall matrix (Sırakaya, 2023). If soluble sugar fractions are removed or valorized separately, the timing of stabilization steps (e.g., drying, milling, extraction) can affect both yield and functional quality. Therefore, supply chain design for food-grade applications may favor shorter storage durations, rapid drying to stable moisture levels, and traceable lot management to ensure consistency. Almond shells are low in moisture and composed primarily of lignocellulosic structural polymers, which provide inherent stability. Shells are typically stockpiled outdoors at hulling facilities or transported to end users for livestock bedding, fuel, or other fiber-based applications. When protected from excessive moisture and managed to prevent compaction, moisture accumulation, and heating, shells can be stored for extended periods (up to a year) with minimal degradation. This stability enables their use in applications such as bioenergy, composite materials, and soil amendment products without strict time constraints between generation and utilization. Overall, while hulls and shells are considerably more stable than high-moisture byproducts such as pomace fractions, their functional stability is context-dependent and shaped by the intended end use. Applications relying primarily on structural carbohydrates (e.g., bioenergy, fiber products, soil amendments) are generally tolerant of extended storage, whereas processes targeting soluble sugar fractions may benefit from shorter storage intervals or controlled storage environments.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Supply and Characteristics

Wine grape production remains a major economic driver for the North San Joaquin Valley, generating more than $400 million in farmgate revenue in 2024, with San Joaquin County alone accounting for over $300 million (Merced County, n.d.; San Joaquin County Agricultural Commissioner / Sealer of Weights & Measures, n.d.; Stanislaus County Agricultural Commissioner, n.d). In recent years, production between white and red wine grapes has been nearly equal in tonnage (350,000 - 400,000 tons/yr each) (U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Statistics Service, & California Department of Food and Agriculture, 2025). Overall wine production in the region has decreased by roughly 20% over the past decade, with 2024 being the smallest crop in more than 20 years (Lodi 411, 2024). This decrease reflects shifts in consumer alcohol preferences and a softening of demand for high volume brands. Table grape production is negligible, representing less than 20 tons annually across the three-county area (U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Statistics Service, & California Department of Food and Agriculture, 2025).

The most important winegrowing area in the region is the Lodi American Viticultural Area (AVA) which is the largest winegrowing region in the United States and is responsible for more than 20% of total wine produced by the state of California and more than 17% of wine produced in America (Caparoso, 2025). In 2024, total grape harvest in the three county region totaled to 757,000 tons (Merced County, n.d.; San Joaquin County Agricultural Commissioner / Sealer of Weights & Measures, n.d.; Stanislaus County Agricultural Commissioner, n.d).

The winemaking process in the North San Joaquin Valley is driven by mature vineyards and long-standing production practices that support the region's role as a high-volume supplier to California's wine industry. Vineyards are commonly 20-50 years old, with many blocks reaching peak productivity between years 7-20, when yields and fruit quality stabilize. The region's warm climate and dependable weather enable consistent ripening: white wine grapes such as Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc are generally harvested from early August through mid-September, while red varieties including Zinfandel, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Merlot are typically picked from mid-September through late October to meet contract specifications for sugar content, color intensity, and flavor preference. Harvest timing and contracted prices are closely tied to sugar accumulation (measured in Brix), with growers and wineries coordinating closely to hit target ranges that align with style, quality tier, and market pricing. Viticultural operations follow a predictable annual cycle that influences labor, equipment demand, and downstream processing timelines and ultimately governs the timing, volume, and perishability of grape pomace generated during harvest. Pruning occurs while vines are dormant from December through February, followed by tying, frost management, and early-season canopy work as temperatures rise. From April through June, growers focus on shoot thinning and positioning, and fruit set, with additional leafing or crop adjustment later in the season to optimize airflow and fruit quality. When Brix levels reach target levels, harvest begins in earnest and initiates rapid winery activities, including grape cluster transport to crush facilities, destemming, grape pressing, juice fermentation, and transfer of wine to tanks or barrels for stabilization and aging. In the North San Joaquin Valley, following harvest, grape batch segregation versus commingling depends on contract terms, wine program objectives, and winery scale. Very large producers such as Gallo, Constellation, and The Wine Group routinely commingle fruit within defined quality tiers or program specifications. Grapes that meet shared criteria, variety, Brix, color, district, and harvest density, are combined into large fermentation lots to optimize throughput and ensure consistent product profiles. Identity preservation is applied only when required by contract, such as for single vineyard designations, specific appellation claims, or premium bottles/labels. Mid-sized and custom-crush operators are more likely to maintain batch separation, especially for smaller wineries or higher-end programs. These facilities often allocate dedicated tanks, small-lot fermenters, or segregated juice streams to preserve traceability from vineyard to bottle and ensure compliance with appellation requirements and market positioning. Some commingling still occurs, particularly for lower-tier blends or spot-market fruit without identity restrictions.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Supply and Characteristics

Mid-sized and custom-crush operators are more likely to maintain batch separation, especially for smaller wineries or higher-end programs. These facilities often allocate dedicated tanks, small-lot fermenters, or segregated juice streams to preserve traceability from vineyard to bottle and ensure compliance with appellation requirements and market positioning. Some commingling still occurs, particularly for lower-tier blends or spot-market fruit without identity restrictions.

Lower-quality fruit or grapes lacking a designated buyer are generally commingled by variety and quality tier to produce consistent bulk wine lots for resale. Federal and California labeling rules allow blending while retaining appellation distinctions, enabling wineries to balance supply variability and meet production targets.

Grape pomace is the solid residue left after winemaking, consisting of skins, seeds, pulp, and sometimes stems that remain once the juice has been pressed. In the case of white wine, skins and seeds are separated from the juice prior to fermentation. For red wine, seeds and skins are recovered after fermentation. There can be significant variability in pomace composition depending on grape varietals, pressing technology, and processing. Additional information on the pomace can be found below in the section entitled 'Pomace fraction' .

Vineyard thinnings, prunings, and removals represent woody biomass generated at different points in the vineyard cycle, primarily composed of canes, cordons, and trunk wood with high lignocellulosic content and low moisture once cured (illustrated above in figure 2-2). While these materials are not the primary focus of this chapter (see subsequent chapter on woody biomass), they represent an additional seasonal and episodic biomass stream that competes for similar land application, composting, or disposal outlets as grape pomace.

Compared to other winegrowing regions in California, production in the Central Valley is skewed towards large and very-large wineries that operate as vertically integrated conglomerates: controlling the entire supply chain including winegrowing, grape hauling, crushing, fermentation, bottling, and waste management (Alston et al., 2019). This structural concentration strongly influences pomace handling. Statewide, the largest vineyard/vineyard holding companies represent less than 1% of producers, but control 32% of total acreage (Alston et al., 2019). Lower land prices in the Central Valley, compared to Napa, Sonoma, and other major wine regions of California, likely skews this distribution further towards very-large producers. The majority of small growers (with <15 acres) together control only a small fraction (under 5%) of total acreage, despite being numerically the majority (Alston et al., 2019). According to Lodi 411, major processor purchases represent 75-80% of crop totals, custom-crush operators handle 15-20% of crop volumes, and grower wineries represent 5-10% of crop volumes (Lodi 411, 2024). Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Wine Grape and Pomace Hauling/Transportation

During harvest season, grape hauling is a logistically challenging endeavor, requiring the movement of hundreds of thousands of tons of grapes during a short window of 12-16 weeks.

Pomace hauling is also a common service provided by grape hauling entities. G3 Enterprises, one of the largest grape hauling companies in California, is also a major hauler of grape pomace statewide, estimated to haul more than 40% of the entire state's grape pomace (G3 Enterprises, Inc., n.d.). G3 Enterprises transports pomace to centralized processing facilities in Livingston, CA or Fresno, CA where it is stored and later processed into animal feed as well as other high value product markets including natural color pigments, nutraceuticals, and other small-market/high-value applications (S. Anderson, personal communication, January 22, 2026).

Grape pomace logistics, storage, and processing are costly. Ensiling pomace rapidly after pressing/fermentation is critical to avoid spoilage. Compared to the grapes, the pomace is more dense, wetter, and trailers may require some manual scraping when dumping. The trucks performing pomace hauling may also require Logistics Insight: A 30-50% Transport Premium Hauling pomace costs 30% to 50% more per ton than hauling fresh grapes (reaching $34-$50/ton ). High water content adds weight and density, while trucks require specialized trailer liners, frequent washouts between runs, and manual scraping during dumping.

Compared to the grapes, the pomace is more dense, wetter, and trailers may require some manual scraping when dumping. liners and need more frequent washouts if also used as back-hauls for field grapes, resulting in higher total hauling costs. Additionally, the routing of these trucks for pomace delivery is more varied, with some going directly to feed lots and others going to storage/processing facilities. Cost-Return studies from UC Davis for the Lodi AVA report grape hauling at around $22/ton (in 2021) for local hauls, which typically refer to distances of 10-15 miles. Given the increased weights/volume (+20-30%, leading to higher fuel costs), slower turnaround times due to truck cleanout, and longer travel distances, it is reasonable to assume that pomace transportation costs would be 30-50% more expensive than grape costs (Murdock et al., 2022). For longer distances (40+ miles), costs may approach $50 per ton depending on routing and washout requirements. Small and mid-size wineries may use the same trailers for grapes and pomace since they do not have a large area to store the pomace. Large wineries have the flexibility of on-site storage and/or transfers using dedicated pomace trailers. In some cases, haulers are able to partially offset pomace transportation costs through backhauling, whereby trucks delivering grapes to wineries are routed to haul pomace on the return trip rather than traveling empty. This practice is most feasible where vineyards, wineries, and pomace receiving sites (e.g., feedlots or land application fields) are geographically aligned and where timing allows immediate loading. While backhauling can reduce empty miles and marginal hauling costs, its applicability is limited by tight harvest schedules, liner and washout requirements, and the need to segregate food-grade grape transport from byproduct hauling. As a result, backhauling reduces spot transportation costs, but does not eliminate the structural cost premium associated with pomace transport.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Pomace Production and Supply

As noted above, grape pomace is the residue after crushing (in the case of white pomace) and after fermentation (in the case of red wine pomace). It is sourced directly from wineries at the end of the crush line, typically transferred from presses or fermentation tanks into hoppers, bins, or truck-mounted tubs for hauling to byproduct markets. Composition varies by wine type: red pomace is fermented with skins and therefore contains lower moisture (often ~55-65%) and higher fiber, free tannins, and residual ethanol, while white pomace is pressed before fermentation and thus has higher moisture (often ~65-75%) and less free tannins. Nutrient profiles for both red and white pomace typically include high neutral-detergent fiber (NDF), crude protein, and residual sugars and extractives that together influence feed or end-use value. There can be significant variability in pomace composition depending on grape varietals, pressing technology and processing. Additionally, pomace, given its high moisture and carbohydrate content, can spoil or mold rapidly without ensiling.

Pomace volumes are directly correlated with the quantities of grapes crushed, yielding approximately 0.25-0.30 lb pomace/lb of grapes crushed for red wine and 0.20-0.25 lb pomace/lb of grapes for white wine (Weis et al., 2025). These yield factors represent industry-average assumptions used for regional material flow estimation and may vary by varietal, press type, and fermentation practice. Red wine and white wine pomace vary significantly due to the fact that white wine pomace is recovered before fermentation and red wine pomace is recovered after fermentation. The presence of the skins, seeds, stems, and pulp during red wine fermentation not only imparts color to the finished wine, but changes the chemical composition of the pomace. Most notably, the presence of the yeast lowers the amount of residual sugars and extractives found in grape skin. High concentrations of tannins can be found on the surface of grape seeds as a means to protect seeds from oxidation. With red wine, seeds are exposed to the fermentation alcohol and therefore lose tannins to the wine. For white wine, the seeds remain separate from the fermentation process and therefore the pomace contains high 'bound' tannins. This creates significant differences in chemical composition, and as will be discussed later, nutritional value. Table x below summarizes the compositional differences between white wine and red wine pomace.

White wine pomace is produced immediately after pressing and is generally wetter and more uniform, while red wine pomace is generated after fermentation and extended skin contact, resulting in greater structural breakdown, higher fiber and lignin content, and elevated spoilage risk once removed from tanks. Because grape processing in the NSJV is highly seasonal and concentrated within a narrow harvest window (generally August through October), pomace generation occurs in short, high-volume pulses that strongly shape downstream handling and utilization pathways. Further, due to the seasonality of the grapes, white wine pomace enters the market in August/September, and red wine pomace becomes available in September/October.

The organizational structure of the grape processing sector strongly influences pomace outcomes. Large vertically integrated wineries and processors-particularly those operating at industrial scale-typically manage pomace through centralized handling systems and long-standing relationships with nearby growers, dairies, or composting operators, often under more stable or annual arrangements rather than spot markets. Interviews with former senior management at major processor subsidiaries indicate that centralized byproduct managers such as G3 Enterprises handle pomace streams from multiple major wine producers in the North San Joaquin Valley (S. Anderson, personal communication, January 22, 2026). These volumes are routinely bunkered and ensiled to preserve feed utility, with pricing and offtake behavior closely tracking regional silage availability and water conditions which affect traditional animal feeds (S. Anderson, personal communication, January 22, 2026). Only a subset of large processors operate fully integrated pomace stabilization and feed-marketing systems; however, these entities possess unique anoxic storage, handling, and logistical capabilities that enable more diversified and high-value end uses. For facilities with integrated stabilization infrastructure and established dairy markets, animal feed is the dominant outlet, supporting year-round utilization as supplies of other silage feedstocks wane. While animal feed represents a smaller share of pomace utilization when averaged across all large processors in the North San Joaquin Valley, processors with integrated handling operations are estimated to route approximately 55-70 percent of their pomace to feed, underscoring the importance of infrastructure and storage rather than processor scale alone. These same operational capabilities also create opportunities for higher-value uses of specific pomace fractions, including natural pigments, nutraceuticals, antioxidant additives, and other specialty chemicals. However, pigment and antioxidant recovery generally requires immediate processing, varietal specificity, and advanced purification capacity, constraining these pathways to a small number of large, technically sophisticated operators and limiting their overall contribution to total pomace utilization (S. Anderson, personal communication, January 22, 2026). Custom crush facilities and smaller estate wineries, by contrast, face tighter logistical constraints: limited space for storage, minimal capital for stabilization infrastructure, and higher per-ton hauling costs. In these cases, pomace is frequently treated as a liability rather than a coproduct, with hauling and disposal costs negotiated on a per-ton basis and subject to seasonal capacity constraints at receiving sites. Unlike almond hulls and shells, which often represent a meaningful revenue stream for processors, grape pomace rarely contributes positively to processor margins under current market conditions, with economic outcomes driven primarily by avoided disposal and compliance costs rather than by commodity value.
