In these operations, utilization of grape pomace is motivated by low-cost, bulk outlets that can absorb large volumes on short notice. Historically and presently, the most common pathways include land application as a soil amendment, livestock feed use (primarily for beef cattle rather than dairies), composting, and limited anaerobic digestion.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Land Application

Direct land application is the dominant utilization pathway for grape pomace in the North San Joaquin Valley, reflecting its low cost, immediacy, and compatibility with vineyard operations. Pomace is typically applied raw or minimally aged to vineyard blocks or nearby agricultural land shortly after crushing, allowing wineries to avoid the costs and logistical challenges associated with transport, drying, or off-site processing. From a nutrient perspective, grape pomace provides organic matter, potassium, and micronutrients, though it is not a balanced fertilizer and is generally applied at agronomic rates to avoid issues related to salinity, oxygen demand, or phytotoxicity. Land application of grape pomace and other winery process solids in San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced Counties falls under the jurisdiction of the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board (CVRWQCB) and has been regulated primarily through conditional waivers of Waste Discharge Requirements (WDRs) rather than individual permits. These conditional waivers address water quality protections but do not constitute solid-waste permitting, distinguishing land application from composting or digestion activities regulated under CalRecycle authority. The most relevant regulatory framework is the Board's General Order and Conditional Waiver for Winery Process Water and Winery Waste Solids, which applies Valley-wide and explicitly identifies land application as a beneficial reuse when conducted under best management practices. Land application is encouraged under the Lodi Rules sustainability certification (Lodi Winegrape Commission, 2022). Overall, land application functions primarily as a cost-avoidance and waste management strategy rather than a value-generating outlet, but it remains the most flexible and scalable option for managing seasonal surges of pomace during harvest.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Animal Feed

Feed use is constrained by high moisture content, rapid microbial degradation, and variable nutritional value, which limit transport distance and require rapid placement or stabilization. As a result, grape pomace is considered a filler feed (S. Anderson, personal communication, January 22, 2026). White wine pomace can be introduced as feed at rates of 5-15% of total ration whereas red wine pomace is lower at 5-10% of total ration (Blasi et al., 2024). In practice, dairies typically utilize on-farm silage inventories first, turning to pomace primarily when alternative silage supplies tighten. White wine pomace is preferred due to higher nutritional content (especially sugars) when compared to other feedstuffs, improved palatability for animals, and stability.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Composting and Anaerobic Digestion

Composting and anaerobic digestion (AD) account for a smaller share of grape pomace utilization in the North San Joaquin Valley than in several other California wine regions due to a combination of structural, economic, and geographic factors. First, the NSJV wine sector is dominated by large-scale, high-throughput processors and custom crush facilities that generate pomace in short, intense seasonal pulses, favoring outlets that can accept material immediately with minimal preprocessing. However, by nature, composting and AD facilities typically have more limited intake rates (due to limited physical space) and require greater feedstock consistency. Second, compared to coastal and North Coast wine regions, the NSJV has historically had fewer permitted composting and AD facilities located in close proximity to wineries, increasing hauling distances and costs for a high-moisture, low-value material. Third, abundant and comparatively inexpensive alternative disposal pathways-particularly direct land application and livestock feed use-have reduced the economic incentive to invest in composting or digestion infrastructure. Finally, regulatory complexity, permitting timelines, and feedstock management requirements for compost and AD have posed higher relative barriers for processors whose core operations are focused on throughput and cost control during the harvest window. Together, these factors have resulted in composting and anaerobic digestion playing a secondary role in pomace management in the NSJV relative to regions where smaller winery scale, tighter land constraints, and closer proximity to organics processing infrastructure make these pathways more competitive. SB 279 has the potential to enable greater on-site composting of grape pomace at smaller independent wineries and custom crush facilities by raising the volumetric thresholds that trigger more stringent composting permit requirements. Importantly, SB 279 modifies solid-waste permitting requirements but does not alter water quality or air quality compliance obligations. For many winery-scale operations in the North San Joaquin Valley, annual pomace volumes fall below these thresholds (now 500 cubic yards), allowing composting activities to proceed under a simplified Policy Update: On-Site Composting Relief (SB 279) SB 279 increases the volumetric exemption threshold for solid-waste composting permits to 500 cubic yards . This lowers administrative barriers and compliance costs, enabling small wineries and custom-crush facilities to compost self-generated pomace on-site starting in the 2026 season.

This regulatory shift lowers compliance costs and reduces administrative complexity, making it more feasible for wineries to compost self-generated pomace and return stabilized material to adjacent vineyards. While practical constraints related to space, labor, and peak harvest logistics remain, SB 279 meaningfully improves the regulatory viability of on-site composting for smaller wineries and could support incremental increases in compost utilization where site conditions and management capacity allow (S. Anderson, personal communication, January 22, 2026). Depending on final rulemaking timelines, these changes could begin to materially affect pomace handling decisions as early as the 2026 growing season. However, it bears noting that the seed fraction in particular is significantly more recalcitrant compared to the other pomace fractions, and either requires milling or end uses that can tolerate long digestion times.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Alternative and Emerging Uses

High value uses for grape pomace are largely focused on upgrading a low-value, high-moisture byproduct into higher-value ingredients or materials, though most remain at the research and pilot stage. One commercially practiced approach is the extraction of grape seed oil, polyphenols, tannins, and dietary fiber for use in nutraceutical, cosmetic, and animal-nutrition applications. Grape seeds are particularly attractive due to their oil content and antioxidant compounds, while skins contain pigments and phenolics with potential functional properties. These pathways can command orders-of-magnitude higher unit values than feed or land application, but require drying, separation, and extraction infrastructure, as well as consistent feedstock quality. The feedstock quality is of paramount importance for pigments, as these pigments need to be recovered as quickly after grape crushing as possible to avoid degradation and yield losses (S. Anderson, personal communication, January 22, 2026). As a result, these high value uses are currently concentrated among a small number of integrated processors/subsidiaries or third-party ingredient manufacturers that possess both the storage and stabilization infrastructure and in-house technical expertise to employ these technologies. Beyond extractives, grape pomace is being explored as a feedstock for biomaterials, bioenergy intermediates, and soil carbon products, including biochar, biocomposites, and fermentation substrates. Research efforts have examined pomace-derived biochar for soil amendment and carbon sequestration, as well as incorporation of pomace fibers into biodegradable packaging or composite materials. Examples of these pathways include pilot-scale human nutrition supplements, and experimental pomace-derived biochar production evaluated through university and private-sector research programs. While technically promising, these applications face scale and economics challenges similar to those observed for other emerging feedstocks: feedstock stability, capital

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Alternative and Emerging Uses

Research efforts have examined pomace-derived biochar for soil amendment and carbon sequestration, as well as incorporation of pomace fibers into biodegradable packaging or composite materials. Examples of these pathways include pilot-scale human nutrition supplements, and experimental pomace-derived biochar production evaluated through university and private-sector research programs. While technically promising, these applications face scale and economics challenges similar to those observed for other emerging feedstocks: feedstock stability, capital

intensity, competition from lower-cost biomass feedstocks, and limited local processing capacity. As with emerging almond coproduct markets, broader adoption will depend on whether these pathways can overcome logistics and processing costs and offer a clear economic advantage over established, low-cost utilization options such as land application, composting, or feed. Overall, the NSJV grape pomace market is best characterized as cost-avoidance driven, geographically constrained, and structurally fragmented. Utilization pathways are shaped less by end-market demand than by proximity, regulatory compliance, and the ability of receiving operations to absorb material during peak harvest periods. While research and pilot efforts continue to explore higher-value uses, including drying, extraction, and bioenergy, these pathways remain limited by scale, capital requirements, and competition from lower-cost disposal alternatives. As with other agricultural byproducts in the region, the future role of grape pomace will depend not only on technological feasibility, but on how regulatory pressures, land availability, and consolidation within the wine industry reshape the economics of byproduct handling.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Pomace Pricing Dynamics and Market Drivers

Unlike other feed commodities (such as almond hulls), grape pomace pricing is not tracked or reported publicly. In the North San Joaquin Valley, pomace used as livestock feed functions primarily as a filler or moisture-balancing feedstock rather than a nutritionally optimized ration. As a result, pricing is typically inferred using proxy feeds rather than direct nutrient composition, with corn silage and almond hulls serving as reference points. Corn silage provides an upper bound due to its higher rumen-available energy and consistent intake, while almond hulls provide a lower bound reflecting a lower-value, high-fiber byproduct. By converting prevailing market prices for these reference feeds into a $/lb of total digestible nutrients (TDN) and applying that value to the estimated TDN content of grape pomace (generally 42-58 percent TDN on a dry-matter basis, depending on red versus white pomace), pomace prices can be expressed on a comparable energy basis. While this approach does not imply that pomace is rationed on a strict nutrient-equivalence basis in practice, it provides a consistent framework for comparing feeds with differing moisture content, digestibility, and intake characteristics without requiring batch-by-batch laboratory analysis, which is rarely performed. The most significant determinant of pomace pricing when used as animal feed is the availability of alternative silage feeds in a given year, with demand increasing during drought periods or years when primary silage feeds (alfalfa, corn silage, almond hulls) are constrained. Industry interviews indicate that pomace pricing closely tracks regional water conditions and silage availability, with dairies

typically prioritizing their own silage supplies and utilizing pomace when those inventories tighten.

Using recent (2024) regional feed prices( approximately $53 per wet ton for corn silage and $74 per wet ton for almond hulls) this methodology yields energy-equivalent pomace values spanning roughly $30 to $50 per wet ton (Merced County, n.d.; San Joaquin County Agricultural Commissioner / Sealer of Weights & Measures, n.d.; Stanislaus County Agricultural Commissioner, n.d).

For many small and mid-scale wineries, however, net realized prices may be zero or negative once hauling, handling, and spoilage risk are accounted for. White wine pomace, produced earlier in the harvest season and retaining higher residual sugar content, typically prices toward the upper end of this range and may approach silage-equivalent values when handled efficiently and marketed through established feed channels. Red wine pomace, generated later in the season after fermentation on the skins, is generally discounted relative to energy equivalence due to intake limitations, higher spoilage risk, and narrower transport windows, placing it closer to the lower end of the range. In practice, final transaction prices reflect a combination of energy benchmarks, seasonality, haul distance, and local byproduct supply conditions, with the silage-and-hulls framework providing a practical basis for price setting rather than a strict nutritional valuation.

Wine grape processing in the NSJV typically peaks between August and October, creating a short-term surge of both white and red wine pomace. Given the region's large production volumes, substantial quantities of organic residuals are generated within a narrow window. This concentration places pressure on wineries, processors, and waste management systems to rapidly handle and redistribute materials before quality degradation occurs. As noted previously, grape pomace begins degrading soon after crushing due to its high moisture content and biological activity.

<!-- image -->

For white wine pomace, spoilage can begin within 12-24 hours under harvest conditions if the material is stockpiled without stabilization. The high moisture content and residual fermentable sugars make the pomace biologically unstable, promoting microbial growth, spontaneous fermentation, odor generation, and potential loss of extractable bioactive compounds. Ensiling is commonly practiced to stabilize the material by rapid acidification under anaerobic conditions, and bale silage studies indicate that ensiling can preserve nutritional and microbial quality of grape pomace for extended storage periods (6-12 months) suitable for ruminant feed use (Romero et al., 2025). Drying is also employed to reduce moisture and prevent microbial degradation, though it is energy-intensive and requires large quantities of scale to be viable. Best practices include rapid pile formation, effective compaction, impermeable covers, weighted sealing systems, and runoff management to prevent oxygen exposure. As with other regional byproducts, storage duration is also shaped by inventory turnover and space constraints, as processors and feedlots generally aim to reduce stockpiles before the subsequent harvest season.

For high-value applications such as pigments, antioxidants, and nutraceutical compounds, degradation through oxidation begins within hours after crushing due to cellular disruption and exposure to oxygen. Polyphenols and other bioactive compounds are present in both skins and seeds; however, once structural integrity is lost, enzymatic oxidation and non-enzymatic reactions can reduce extractable quality within hours if not controlled. This also limits the use of drying and other storage (Guaita et al., 2023). Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Seasonality, Stability, and Storage Constraints of Wine Grape Pomace

Polyphenols and other bioactive compounds are present in both skins and seeds; however, once structural integrity is lost, enzymatic oxidation and non-enzymatic reactions can reduce extractable quality within hours if not controlled. This also limits the use of drying and other storage (Guaita et al., 2023). As a result, these applications typically require rapid processing, controlled atmosphere handling, or immediate extraction (S. Anderson, personal communication, January 22,

2026). Extended wet storage without stabilization is generally incompatible with premium extractive markets. Red wine pomace is typically somewhat more stable in the short term than white pomace because most fermentable sugars have already been consumed during alcoholic fermentation. However, it remains a high-moisture organic material and will deteriorate under aerobic conditions if unmanaged. Although red wine pomace retains measurable polyphenol content, fermentation and extended skin contact can result in oxidation, polymerization, and binding of phenolic compounds, reducing their extractability and suitability for certain high-value applications. The same ensiling and storage practices apply, with red wine pomace retaining higher nutritional content when ensiled, although reduced residual sugars may result in less vigorous lactic fermentation unless co-ensiled with carbohydrate-rich substrates (De Bellis et al., 2022). Overall, the strong seasonality of grape processing in the NSJV necessitates coordinated, regionally integrated solutions for byproduct management. Infrastructure for rapid stabilization, proximity between processors and valorization pathways, and alignment with agricultural demand (e.g., soil amendments or feed uses) are critical to improving resource recovery. Addressing these temporal and

logistical constraints will be central to advancing circular bioeconomy strategies within the NSJV grape sector.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Supply and Characteristics

Olive production in the North San Joaquin Valley (NSJV) is modest in total acreage and tonnage relative to grapes and almonds. County crop reports list olive production using varying terminology: 'Olives, Processing' in San Joaquin County, 'Olives, Oil' in Stanislaus County, and aggregated miscellaneous categories in Merced County. The limited number of processors within the three-county study area results in crop report categories that aggregate data to protect processor confidentiality. Multiple independent data sources indicate that these county crop report categories reflect oil olive production. USDA NASS estimates place statewide table olive production at approximately 40,000 tons in 2024 on roughly 12,200 bearing acres (United States Department of Agriculture, National Agricultural Statistics Service, 2024) , with industry data from the California Olive Committee indicating that more than 90% of table olive acreage is concentrated in Tulare County and Sacramento Valley counties (California Olive Committee, n.d.).  Olive acreage expansion in the North San Joaquin Valley has been driven primarily by oil-oriented varietals such as Arbequina, Arbosana, and Koroneiki, which are utilized in super-high-density orchards and are well suited for mechanical harvesting and continuous-flow oil extraction (Ferguson et al., n.d.). In contrast, traditional table olive varietals such as Manzanillo and Sevillano, characterized by larger fruit size and curing-oriented processing, are geographically concentrated outside the NSJV (Ferguson et al., n.d.). Therefore, oil olive production in San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced Counties is interpreted to represent the vast majority of production (>95%). Understanding the end use of the olives is critical for the purposes of this report, as the byproduct and waste profiles for table olive vs oil production are distinct.

Reported and estimated olive tonnage across the NSJV reflects this oil-dominant structure and exhibits variability from year to year driven by orchard age and alternate year bearing cycle. San Joaquin County accounts for the largest share of regional production, with reported annual tonnage fluctuating between approximately 10,000 and 20,000 tons in recent years. Stanislaus County production has increased steadily, from roughly 4,800 tons in 2021 to nearly 8,800 tons in 2024, consistent with expansion of super-high-density oil olive orchards.

Based on typical orchard development timelines and regional yields, Merced County olive production is estimated to have increased from fewer than 100 tons in 2021 to approximately 700 tons in 2024 as orchards transitioned toward commercial bearing. Across the three counties, total olive production ranged from approximately 15,000-23,000 tons annually between 2021 and 2023, increasing to nearly 29,000 tons in 2024. Much of this increase in recent years is owed to the maturation of orchards entering production phase. Olive harvest in the NSJV is highly seasonal and tightly coupled to mill processing capacity, resulting in short-duration, high-intensity material flows. Harvest typically occurs from late September through November, with oil olives harvested to align fruit maturity with mill availability rather than grower discretion. Super-high-density orchard systems dominate the region and are mechanically harvested, with fruit delivered to mills within hours to preserve oil quality (Ferguson et al., n.d.). This results in harvest windows on the order of six to ten weeks, during which large volumes of fruit are delivered to a small number of centralized oil mills in San Joaquin and Stanislaus Counties. Limited local milling capacity in Merced County necessitates cross-county hauling, further reinforcing the importance of coordinated scheduling and rapid throughput. Because olive production in the NSJV is almost entirely oil-oriented, wet olive pomace is the dominant byproduct of concern. Olive oil milling typically generates approximately 0.6-0.9 tons of wet pomace per ton of olives processed, depending on extraction technology (Ammar & Cherif, 2017). Applying this range to NSJV production suggests regional pomace generation of roughly 13,000-20,000 tons annually between 2021 and 2023, increasing to approximately 25,000 tons in 2024. Pomace consists of olive pulp, skins, and pits and is produced at centralized mills during a short harvest window, making it spatially concentrated but highly seasonal. Orchard management generates comparatively minor biomass streams relative to processing byproducts, and these streams are episodic rather than continuous. Annual pruning during winter dormancy produces small quantities of woody biomass, typically well under one ton per acre in young and moderate-vigor orchards. In contrast to vineyards, olives do not undergo routine in-season fruit thinning, and associated green biomass generation is minimal. Full orchard removals occur on multi-decade cycles and can generate substantial woody material but are spatially dispersed and infrequent. As a result, olive pomace remains the dominant and most predictable biomass stream associated with olive production in the NSJV, with implications for aggregation, handling, and potential valorization focused at the mill scale rather than the orchard scale.

Olive material flows in the North San Joaquin Valley are shaped by a small number of centralized processing facilities that largely determine harvest timing, hauling patterns, and byproduct generation. Unlike grapes, which are delivered to dozens of crushing facilities of varying size and operational models, oil olives in the region are processed at a limited number of mills, including one large industrial-scale facility designed specifically for super-high-density (SHD) orchards. These industrial mills often operate a two-stage extraction system designed to minimize wastewater volumes but result in higher kg/kg pomace yields. Other olive mills are specifically designed for custom milling services with segregated processing lines and lot tracing to maintain single varietals, lots, and organic status. This concentration of capacity results in highly synchronized harvest windows and predictable within-season material surges, though total annual volumes fluctuate due to alternate bearing years. The majority of locally produced olives are processed for oil, with fruit delivered directly from orchards to mills and entering continuous-flow extraction systems with minimal intermediate handling.

Figure 3-3. Illustration of material flows and current end uses of oil olives and olive byproduct fractions.

Because processing capacity is centralized and harvest is tightly scheduled to align with mill throughput, byproduct generation is similarly predictable over this harvest period. Industrial-scale oil mills generate large volumes of wet pomace over a six- to ten-week harvest period, with daily output correlating to input capacity. Smaller and custom mills handle lower volumes but may manage more heterogeneous fruit streams, including organic or specialty varietals that require lot segregation and additional traceability controls. These operational differences influence handling practices but do not materially alter the overall mass balance: nearly all fruit delivered to oil mills is processed into oil and wet pomace, with limited secondary waste streams beyond leaves and minor debris removed during cleaning.

Table olive processing is present within the region but is distinct from oil milling and is not directly proportional to local acreage. A single large table olive facility located in the region sources fruit from across California (especially Tulare county), meaning that brining, curing, and pit management activities may occur within the three-county area even when production acreage is concentrated elsewhere. As a result, oil-oriented material flows dominate at the orchard level in the North San Joaquin Valley, while both oil pomace and table olive residues may be generated at specific processing sites. content:
Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Olive and Pomace Hauling/Transportation

Olive hauling in the North San Joaquin Valley is characterized by short-haul, time-sensitive transport from orchards to a small number of centralized oil mills, with logistics structured to prioritize rapid delivery and processing during harvest. Olives for oil are typically harvested and transported within hours to preserve oil quality, limiting the practical Just-in-Time Logistics: The Rapid Milling Window Unlike almonds or grapes, harvested oil olives degrade via oxidation within hours . Super-high-density (SHD) orchards utilize mechanical harvesters and double-gondola trailers (25-28 ton payloads) operating within a tight 5 to 30-mile radius , with harvest timing strictly dictated by mill intake capacity.

hauling radius and favoring nearby mills in San Joaquin and Stanislaus Counties. Because olive oil quality degrades rapidly after harvest due to oxidation and fermentation, often within a few hours, the logistics network is tighter and more urgent than for shelf-stable crops such as almonds or walnuts. Transport distances from orchard to mill commonly range from approximately 5-30 miles, though longer hauls may occur in Merced County, where limited local milling infrastructure requires fruit to be delivered to neighboring counties. Oil olives are typically hauled in double gondola trailers (G3 Enterprises, n.d.): large, open-top metal bins with V-shaped bottoms that allow rapid gravity unloading at the mill. These trailers accommodate high payloads (often 25-28 tons per load) and support rapid turnaround during peak harvest periods.

Hauling and harvest scheduling are closely coordinated with mill intake capacity to avoid queuing and fruit degradation, and delivery arrangements are typically governed by formal marketing agreements rather than informal hauling contracts. Olive harvest and delivery in the North San Joaquin Valley are dictated by mill capacity rather than grower discretion or optimal ripeness (in the case of Brix for grapes). Growers typically operate under dedicated delivery or custom milling arrangements in which mills assign specific intake windows to align harvest timing with available processing capacity. As a result, harvest scheduling is highly coordinated and time-sensitive, with limited ability to store fruit prior to processing. This mill-centered structure also concentrates responsibility for pomace handling and disposal at the processing facility rather than the orchard. Contracts commonly require strict lot identification and traceability, with truck drivers carrying documentation linking each load to specific orchard blocks to support organic certification and extra-virgin designation. As with grape hauling, peak harvest weeks create intense but short-lived demand for trucks and drivers, with limited flexibility to delay transport.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Olive and Pomace Hauling/Transportation

This mill-centered structure also concentrates responsibility for pomace handling and disposal at the processing facility rather than the orchard. Contracts commonly require strict lot identification and traceability, with truck drivers carrying documentation linking each load to specific orchard blocks to support organic certification and extra-virgin designation. As with grape hauling, peak harvest weeks create intense but short-lived demand for trucks and drivers, with limited flexibility to delay transport.

Hauling services for olive fruit are provided either by vertically integrated operators with dedicated internal fleets or by specialized third-party agricultural haulers contracted for the harvest window. Larger, vertically integrated producers and mills, particularly in San Joaquin and Stanislaus Counties, often maintain their own truck fleets to ensure control over timing and quality, while smaller growers rely on custom haulers serving multiple orchards and mills during the season. Unlike grape hauling, where wineries may accept fruit over extended hours and hold loads briefly, olive mills generally require just-in-time delivery, increasing reliance on predictable, repeat routes rather than long-distance or opportunistic hauling. Coordination between growers, haulers, and mills is therefore tighter, with fewer options for rerouting fruit once harvest begins.

In super-high-density olive production systems, which dominate olive acreage in the North San Joaquin Valley, harvested fruit is mechanically collected and delivered directly to oil mills. No sorting into table versus oil streams occurs, and virtually all harvested olives are processed for oil. Intake handling is limited to removal of leaves and foreign material, which does not materially alter fruit mass flows. Olive oil processing allows very broad acceptability from a fruit quality perspective, resulting in very minimal cull or sorting losses.

Transportation of olive pomace differs from fruit hauling and is typically handled by the same entities responsible for byproduct management rather than by orchard-level haulers. Pomace is generated at mills and is rarely transported using the same equipment as fruit delivery; instead, it is moved using front-end loaders and end-dump trailers operated by mills, affiliated growers, or contracted waste and compost haulers. Transport distances for pomace are generally short, often less than 5-15 miles, reflecting the material's high moisture content, rapid degradation, and preference for nearby land application or composting sites. Where mills are vertically integrated with surrounding farmland, pomace may be managed internally and may not enter the commercial hauling market at all. For independent mills without adjacent land or permitted outlets, reliance on third-party haulers becomes critical, and the availability of nearby disposal or reuse sites can be a limiting factor during peak processing periods.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Pomace Production and Supply

Olive pomace is the primary solid residual generated from olive oil production and consists of olive pulp, skins, pits, and residual moisture remaining after oil extraction. Literature values indicate that olive pomace can represent a substantial share of incoming olive mass, with this analysis applying a conversion factor of 0.87 tons of pomace per ton of olives processed based on Ammar and Cherif (2017). This makes olive production volume a useful proxy for estimating the scale of potentially available pomace in the Northern San Joaquin Valley. Based on available county crop data and correspondence with the Merced County Agricultural Commissioner's office, estimated olive pomace production across Merced, San Joaquin, and Stanislaus Counties ranged from approximately 13,600 to 25,200 tons per year between 2021 and 2024. San Joaquin County is the dominant source of regional olive pomace, accounting for the majority of estimated supply in most years. In 2024, San Joaquin County generated an estimated 16,878 tons of pomace, followed by Stanislaus County with approximately 7,686 tons and Merced County with approximately 600 tons. Combined, the three-county region produced an estimated 25,165 tons of olive pomace in 2024. The available data also suggest meaningful year-to-year variability in olive production and associated pomace supply. This variability is important for supply planning because olive pomace availability is tied closely to annual harvest volume and processing activity. Any project or end-use pathway relying on olive pomace would likely need to account for seasonal concentration during the olive processing period, as well as annual fluctuations in supply. Historical data prior to 2021 are incomplete for the full three-county region because county crop data were not available for Merced and Stanislaus Counties before 2021. As a result, 2017-2020 estimates reflect San Joaquin County only and should be interpreted as an incomplete regional baseline rather than a full estimate of Northern San Joaquin Valley supply.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Pomace Utilization and Market Structure

Olive pomace in the North San Joaquin Valley is managed primarily as a regional byproduct rather than a traded commodity stream. Generated during oil extraction and consisting of skins, pulp, pits, residual oil, and moisture, pomace must move quickly to an outlet due to its high moisture content (typically ~55-65%) and surge in quantity produced during harvest. In wet form, pomace has a limited storage window, typically days to a few weeks depending on temperature, before spoilage, heating, or odor issues emerge. While it ferments more slowly than grape pomace due to lower sugar content and the presence of antimicrobial phenolics, it still requires active management and is rarely stockpiled long-term without ensiling or blending. However, compared to grape pomace, there is higher material stability allowing some additional flexibility in transportation. Nonetheless, olive processing mills prioritize nearby outlets to minimize transportation costs and avoid deterioration. Public sustainability reporting from major California producers indicates that a significant share of pomace is directed into livestock feed and composting pathways, with mills emphasizing 'zero waste' operations and integration with local agricultural partners (California Olive Ranch, n.d.). Based on regional infrastructure and documented practices, it is estimated that roughly half of NSJV pomace is utilized as cattle or dairy feed, approximately 30% is composted or land applied as a soil amendment, and a smaller share (10-20%) enters secondary oil recovery markets or energy uses depending on commodity pricing and logistics. Transportation and disposal economics play a central role in determining these outcomes. Because pomace is heavy and water-laden, hauling costs per unit of usable dry matter are high, which generally limits economical transport to a radius of roughly 50-75 miles unless the material is dried. Drying, however, requires additional capital, energy, and infrastructure, and is typically only justified if the pomace is destined for higher-value secondary oil extraction or fuel markets. In practice, many mills coordinate just-in-time pickups during harvest, aligning truck movements with dairy feed demand or compost facility intake capacity. Some dairies may ensile pomace in combination with other feedstocks (e.g., corn silage or almond hulls) to stabilize it for later use, but this requires space, equipment, and ration planning. The perishability of the material therefore reinforces localized, relationship-based contracting rather than open-market trading. Unlike almond hulls, which function as a standardized and widely traded feed commodity, olive pomace operates within localized, partnership-driven markets. The nutritional profile contains moderate fat, high fiber, and low protein, limits the ration inclusion rates and makes it an opportunistic feed (Scicutella et al., 2024). Many mills rely on recurring agreements with nearby dairies or compost operators to manage predictable seasonal volumes, sometimes integrating pomace with manure management systems to produce stabilized compost.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Pomace Utilization and Market Structure

Unlike almond hulls, which function as a standardized and widely traded feed commodity, olive pomace operates within localized, partnership-driven markets. The nutritional profile contains moderate fat, high fiber, and low protein, limits the ration inclusion rates and makes it an opportunistic feed (Scicutella et al., 2024). Many mills rely on recurring agreements with nearby dairies or compost operators to manage predictable seasonal volumes, sometimes integrating pomace with manure management systems to produce stabilized compost.

Secondary oil extraction offers a technically proven pathway to increase value recovery from olive pomace, particularly in two-phase systems that retain higher residual oil content. This practice is common in Mediterranean producing regions, where aggregated pomace volumes often reach hundreds of thousands of tons annually. However, the modest regional scale of olive production in the NSJV, combined with the high moisture content and concentrated seasonal generation of Scale & Processing Barriers: Secondary Oil Extraction While common in Europe, secondary solvent extraction of pomace oil faces major economic hurdles in the NSJV. Recovering residual oil requires drying pomace down to <10% moisture before hexane extraction-an energy-intensive process that is hard to justify given the region's modest regional pomace volume ( 20-25 kT/yr ).

pomace, likely constrains economic feasibility of standalone solvent extraction facilities without co-location or integration with other biomass streams. To recover this residual oil, the pomace must first be dried to less than 10% moisture to be compatible with the solvent extraction process. The dried pomace is then extracted with nonpolar solvents, such as hexane, to recover the oil which is marketed as olive pomace oil (Rifat et al., 2023). Olive pomace oil is marketed differently than olive oil and typically competes with other oils such as canola or sunflower. Given these high operating costs, it is assumed only a minor share of pomace goes towards secondary oil extraction when commodity prices make this viable. In summary, olive pomace lacks a standardized commodity market and functions primarily as a localized byproduct stream whose movement is governed by disposal economics rather than competitive pricing.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Alternative and Emerging Uses

In addition to established feed, compost, and secondary oil recovery pathways, a growing body of research and pilot activity is focused on higher-value extraction and bioproduct applications for olive pomace. Of particular interest is the recovery of phenolic compounds which have demonstrated value in nutraceutical, functional food, and cosmetic markets (Zhao et al., 2022). Academic and European pilot projects have demonstrated technical feasibility using ultrasound-assisted, microwave-assisted, pressurized liquid, and other 'green' solvent extraction methods to isolate these compounds from wet pomace (Chanioti et al., 2021). Other research has shown potential for use as a binder for asphalt Zhang et al., 2022). While these technologies are scientifically validated and align with circular bioeconomy objectives, they remain limited in commercial deployment within California due to scale constraints, capital requirements, and the logistical challenges associated with handling a seasonal, high-moisture feedstock. The small number of olive oil mills in the region does create structural advantages for pilot deployment, as pomace generation is highly centralized and occurs in predictable, short-duration pulses aligned with harvest throughput. This concentration reduces aggregation barriers relative to more distributed byproduct streams (e.g. wine pomace). However, the modest total regional volume and compressed processing window may limit the economic viability of capital-intensive systems unless co-located with mills or integrated with complementary feedstocks to improve year-round utilization. From a systems perspective, olive byproduct management in the NSJV is characterized by centralized generation, seasonal intensity, modest total scale, and strong dependence on localized agricultural

outlets. These characteristics reduce aggregation barriers but limit the economic viability of capital-intensive standalone processing technologies unless integrated with other biomass streams or co-located at mill sites.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Table Olive Processing

Table olive processing generates a distinct waste profile compared to olive oil milling, consisting primarily of high-salinity wastewater (from brining, lye treatment, washing, and curing), olive pits, and residual flesh solids removed during pitting and sorting. Depending on varietal and processing steps, total wastewater generated can range between 240 gal/ton to 1,400 gal/ton (Rincón-Llorente et al., 2018). The wastewater stream is characterized by elevated chemical oxygen demand (COD), dissolved salts, and organic compounds, which make discharge and treatment complex and tightly regulated under regional water quality standards. Because brine volumes can be substantial and seasonal, processors must either invest in on-site treatment systems, such as evaporation, distillation, biological treatment, or energy-integrated systems like pit-fueled boilers, or secure permitted off-site disposal capacity. Siting these facilities presents logistical challenges due to odor concerns, truck traffic, air permitting for combustion systems, wastewater discharge restrictions, and proximity to municipal infrastructure. As a result, large table olive processors often rely on vertically integrated, capital-intensive treatment and energy recovery systems, while smaller facilities may face higher

per-unit compliance and disposal costs. A notable example of integrated byproduct utilization within California's olive processing sector is Musco Family Olive Co.'s energy recovery system. According to public reporting, Musco combusts olive pits in on-site burners to generate thermal energy, which is transferred via a heat-transfer fluid to a brine boiler that distills process wastewater (American Society of Mechanical Engineers, n.d.). Waste heat from the system is further utilized to dry solids separated from On-Site Circularity: Olive Pit Energy Musco Family Olive Co. combusts olive pits in on-site boilers to generate thermal energy, which distills high-salinity process wastewater. The resulting steam drives an engine that produces ~500 kWh per hour (~50% of the facility's electricity needs), showcasing a closed-loop system that cuts grid power rely and eliminates waste.

The resulting pressurized steam powers a steam engine to generate electricity, supplying approximately 500 kWh per hour-roughly half of the facility's operational electricity demand for sorting, pitting, canning, and packing operations (American Society of the wastewater stream. This closed-loop configuration illustrates how pits and wastewater can be integrated into an industrial energy and treatment system, reducing disposal needs while offsetting grid electricity use. While such capital-intensive systems are most feasible at large, vertically integrated processing facilities, they demonstrate the technical potential for energy recovery and internal circularity within the olive sector.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Seasonality, Stability, and Storage Constraints of Olive Byproduct Streams

Olive oil processing in the NSJV typically occurs between October and January, when olives are harvested and transported rapidly to mills for processing. As noted previously, because olive fruit quality deteriorates quickly after harvest, milling generally occurs within hours, resulting in a concentrated surge of pomace generation during the harvest period. As with other agricultural processing streams in the region, this short processing window creates a seasonal pulse of organic residuals that must be managed rapidly. Olive pomace-composed of skins, pulp, pits, and residual oil-is produced in large quantities over a relatively short period, placing pressure on processors and downstream outlets to absorb material quickly during peak milling activity.

Figure 3-5. Seasonal dynamics of olive pomace generation (flow, right axis) and inventory levels (stock, left axis) in the NSJV region.

<!-- image -->

Olive pomace is a high-moisture organic material, typically containing 55-65 percent water depending on extraction technology. Compared to grape pomace, the material is somewhat more stable due to lower residual sugar content and the presence of phenolic compounds. However the material remains biologically active. Microbial activity and oxidation can lead to heating, odor generation, and quality degradation if the pomace is stockpiled for extended periods under aerobic conditions. Under typical NSJV harvest conditions, untreated pomace is generally managed within days to weeks unless active stabilization measures are employed. Several approaches are used to extend storage life and improve handling logistics. Drying is sometimes used to reduce moisture content and enable use as livestock feed or fuel, though it requires energy inputs and sufficient processing scale to be economically viable. At the scales of production in the valley, drying to the point required for pomace oil extraction is not believed to be a current practice. In some cases, livestock operators incorporate olive pomace into mixed silage piles with other feedstocks, which can stabilize the material through anaerobic fermentation and allow for longer-term feed utilization. Composting operations may also blend pomace with green waste or manure to balance carbon and nitrogen ratios while improving aeration. However, compared to grape pomace systems that may involve centralized ensiling and storage infrastructure, olive pomace handling in the region is typically more decentralized and closely coordinated with local agricultural partners. Overall, because wet pomace is heavy relative to its dry matter value and expensive to transport long distances, most material flows remain geographically constrained. As a result, successful pomace management depends heavily on proximity between mills and receiving operations capable of absorbing large seasonal volumes, reinforcing localized circular flows within the region's agricultural economy.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Supply and Characteristics

Processing tomatoes are a major specialty crop across the North San Joaquin Valley (NSJV). Unlike fresh-market tomatoes, which are harvested and handled for direct consumption, processing tomatoes are grown specifically for industrial conversion into tomato paste, diced tomatoes, peeled tomatoes, sauces, and other shelf-stable tomato products. Across the three-county region, total processing tomato production typically ranges from approximately 1.8 to 2.4 million tons per year, representing one of the largest annual wet biomass streams in the NSJV agricultural economy n.d.; Stanislaus County Agricultural Commissioner, n.d).

(Merced County, n.d.; San Joaquin County Agricultural Commissioner / Sealer of Weights & Measures, In 2024, the three-county region produced approximately 2.18 million tons of processing tomatoes, including about 1.02 million tons in Merced County, 800,000 tons in San Joaquin County, and 355,000 tons in Stanislaus County (AI Institute for Next Generation Food Systems, n.d.; Merced County, n.d.; San Joaquin County Agricultural Commissioner / Sealer of Weights & Measures, n.d.; Stanislaus County Agricultural Commissioner, n.d). Processing tomatoes account for the overwhelming majority of tomatoes harvested in the region, typically representing approximately 93% to 95% of total tomato tonnage (Merced County, n.d.; San Joaquin County Agricultural Commissioner / Sealer of Weights & Measures, n.d.; Stanislaus County Agricultural Commissioner, n.d). As a result, the tomato by-product stream in the NSJV is primarily associated with industrial tomato processing rather than fresh-market packing. Processing tomatoes are harvested on a whole-fruit, field-weight basis and transported directly to processing facilities. The harvested tomato fruit consists primarily of water, soluble solids, fiber, skins, seeds, and pulp. Because the crop is highly perishable and has a very high moisture content, harvested tomatoes are generally delivered to processors rapidly after harvest rather than being stored for extended periods. This differs from tree nut crops such as walnuts, where harvested biomass can be separated into relatively stable dry fractions after hulling, drying, and cracking. Tomato processing instead produces a wet, seasonally concentrated stream of by-products generated during washing, sorting, peeling, pulping, evaporation, and finishing operations.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Supply and Characteristics

Because the crop is highly perishable and has a very high moisture content, harvested tomatoes are generally delivered to processors rapidly after harvest rather than being stored for extended periods. This differs from tree nut crops such as walnuts, where harvested biomass can be separated into relatively stable dry fractions after hulling, drying, and cracking. Tomato processing instead produces a wet, seasonally concentrated stream of by-products generated during washing, sorting, peeling, pulping, evaporation, and finishing operations.

The dominant processing pathway in the region is tomato paste production. According to the UC Davis Byproduct Database, the majority of processing tomatoes in the NSJV are directed to paste, although the share varies substantially by county. Approximately 55% to 60% of processing tomatoes in San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties are used for paste production, while nearly 85% of Merced County processing tomatoes are directed to paste. It is also important to note that tomatoes grown in other counties are processed within the three-county region, resulting in byproduct volumes that do not necessarily match with volumes of in-county cultivation. The remaining volume is primarily used for peeled, diced tomato production, sauces, and other processed tomato products. A small fraction is rejected or discarded due to quality, field damage, or off-specification conditions. These processing pathways are important because they determine both the quantity and character of the tomato by-product stream. Paste production generally produces tomato pomace composed of skins, seeds, fibrous pulp, and residual soluble material separated during pulping and finishing. This material generally has a lower moisture content compared to peeling operations. Peeling operations generate additional wet residues, including peels, trim, and slurry-like material removed during preparation of peeled or diced tomato products. Because different product lines separate tomato solids in different ways, the total by-product volume cannot be estimated reliably from regional tomato tonnage alone without also considering the fraction of tomatoes routed to paste, peeling, and other processing uses. Additionally, processing route (paste, peeling) results in different moisture content for the resulting pomace. For the purposes of this analysis, tomato by-products are treated as wet processing residues generated from the industrial tomato stream. Based on processor-reported estimates, approximately 2-7% (depending on processing method) of inbound processing tomato tonnage may be generated as pomace or comparable wet by-product material across processing operations (J. Schneider, personal communication, May 29, 2026). Applying this factor to the three-county processing tomato supply indicates that a typical regional crop of 1.8 to 2.4 million tons per year could generate approximately 90,000 to 120,000 tons of wet tomato by-product annually. Using 2024 county production volumes, the estimated wet byproduct stream would be approximately 51,000 tons in Merced County, 40,000 tons in San Joaquin County, and 17,750 tons in Stanislaus County, for a combined regional total of approximately 109,000 tons. It is important to note that these wet byproduct and pomace estimates are based on the volumes of tomatoes grown in the three county regions. In practice, additional tomatoes are sourced from neighboring counties and the above estimates would likely be lower than the actual volumes available. These estimates should be interpreted as order-of-magnitude feedstock estimates rather than precise measured values.

It is important to note that these wet byproduct and pomace estimates are based on the volumes of tomatoes grown in the three county regions. In practice, additional tomatoes are sourced from neighboring counties and the above estimates would likely be lower than the actual volumes available. These estimates should be interpreted as order-of-magnitude feedstock estimates rather than precise measured values.

By-product generation depends on processor configuration, tomato quality, product mix, peeling method, moisture content, solids recovery efficiency, and whether residual slurry streams are captured, reused, land-applied, or treated as wastewater-like material. Nevertheless, the scale of processing tomato production in the NSJV indicates that tomato by-products represent a substantial, recurring, and geographically concentrated wet biomass stream.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Summary of Material Flows and Use Cases

County crop reports record tomato production as harvested tomato tonnage, which already includes the whole fruit delivered to processors. The key analytical step for tomato by-products is therefore not reconstructing the whole crop, but allocating the harvested tomato stream across processing pathways and estimating the fraction converted into wet residual material.

For this analysis, the 2024 NSJV processing tomato crop is estimated at approximately 2.18 million tons. Applying county-level product allocation patterns indicates that most of this material enters paste production, particularly in Merced County. Paste production is expected to be the principal source of tomato pomace, while peeling and diced tomato production generate additional wet residues such as peels, trim, and slurry. Assuming a 5% wet by-product generation factor is applied across the full processing tomato stream, the region produces approximately 109,000 tons of wet tomato by-product in 2024.

Tomato pomace and related processing residues are wet, dense, and biologically active. Their high moisture content reduces long-distance transport feasibility and limits storage duration without stabilization. As a result, tomato by-product utilization is likely to be shaped by proximity to processors, seasonal processing schedules, access to nearby livestock or compost markets, and the ability of processors or third-party handlers to manage wet organic material quickly during the harvest and processing season. From a resource-recovery perspective, tomato by-products can contain valuable fibers, seeds, residual sugars, oils, pigments such as lycopene, and nutrients. However, the near-term market for the bulk stream is likely to be dominated by lower-value outlets such as animal feed, composting, land application, anaerobic digestion, or other wet organic waste management pathways unless the material is dried, fractionated, or otherwise stabilized. Only one processor in the greater Central Valley region operates drying equipment, enabling them to sell into the pet food market which commands significantly higher value than cattle feed. Because drying wet tomato residues is energy intensive, higher-value applications are most feasible where processors can separate targeted fractions, use waste heat, or integrate by-product management with existing wastewater, energy, or feed systems. Wastewater and wet residual management represent a distinct but closely related constraint in tomato processing. In addition to pomace, processors generate substantial volumes of wet waste material that may include stems, leaves, organic, and inorganic materials, wash water solids, and other suspended organic residues. Depending on harvesting and processing techniques, wet waste can be a major contributor to total suspended solids (TSS) and biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) in seasonal processing wastewater (J. Schneider, personal communication, May 29, 2026). Much of this material is currently directed to composting rather than higher-value recovery pathways. Although anaerobic digestion is conceptually attractive for high-moisture organic residues, processors indicated that the intermittent nature of the tomato processing season and the scale required for economic digestion make standalone digestion difficult to justify under current conditions (J. Schneider, personal communication, May 29, 2026). The City of Modesto also illustrates the importance of municipal infrastructure in shaping wastewater management and ensuring compliance. During the canning season (mid-June - mid-October), the City of Modesto operates a separate segregated sewer line for wastewater generated from several fruit and vegetable processors (including tomato processing) to avoid fouling and overload issues in the conventional municipal wastewater system. This seasonal flow can reach millions of gallons per day and is routed to retention ponds where solids can settle before further management. Processors operating within this system may be subject to unique water permits and seasonal discharge requirements. This segregated approach is unique compared to other fruit and vegetable processing cities/regions.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Tomato Hauling/Transportation

Transportation of processing tomatoes from fields to processing facilities is an operationally critical component of the tomato supply chain. The crop is mechanically harvested at high volume, loaded into bulk trailers, and transported directly to canneries or paste plants where it enters washing, sorting, peeling, crushing, pulping, evaporation, or other processing operations. This makes hauling one of the most time-sensitive steps in the tomato value chain (California Tomato Growers Association, n.d.).

Processing tomato logistics are shaped by the combination of high moisture content, a compressed processing season, and very large daily throughput requirements. Tomatoes are harvested and transported on a wet, whole-fruit basis, meaning that nearly the entire delivered weight is water-rich biomass. Some vines and green waste are usually present as well. Because the fruit cannot be stored for long periods without quality deterioration, processors must coordinate field harvest schedules, truck availability, plant intake capacity, and product-line demand on a daily or even hourly basis during the processing season. This creates the need for a continuous and tightly synchronized logistics system.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Tomato Hauling/Transportation

Tomatoes are harvested and transported on a wet, whole-fruit basis, meaning that nearly the entire delivered weight is water-rich biomass. Some vines and green waste are usually present as well. Because the fruit cannot be stored for long periods without quality deterioration, processors must coordinate field harvest schedules, truck availability, plant intake capacity, and product-line demand on a daily or even hourly basis during the processing season. This creates the need for a continuous and tightly synchronized logistics system.

In the North San Joaquin Valley, hauling distances are strongly influenced by the location of major tomato-processing facilities and the economics of moving high-moisture fruit. Processing plants in and near the region, including facilities in Modesto, Stockton, Oakdale, Los Banos, and Santa Nella, serve as major aggregation points for tomatoes grown across the three county region. Morning Star's 2025 industry statistics identify major paste and tomato-processing capacity at Los Banos, Santa Nella, Stockton, Oakdale, and other Central Valley locations, with California as a whole producing approximately 96% of U.S. processed tomatoes and representing roughly one-third of the global market (The Morning Star Company, 2025). The same source lists major hourly paste-processing capacity at facilities such as Santa Nella, Los Banos, Stockton, and Oakdale, illustrating the degree to which regional tomato logistics are organized around a limited number of high-throughput processing plants (The Morning Star Company, 2025). Because processing tomatoes have low value per unit of wet weight relative to their transportation burden, growers and processors generally favor relatively short field-to-plant hauls where possible. Long-distance hauling is technically feasible but economically unattractive unless required by crop contracting, plant capacity constraints, weather, harvest timing, or regional supply-demand imbalances. As a result, tomato-processing infrastructure functions as both a market outlet and a logistical anchor: acreage tends to be planned around the ability to deliver large volumes of tomatoes to a suitable plant within the required harvest and quality window. Hauling arrangements are typically embedded in grower-processor contracting structures. Processing tomato acreage is commonly grown under contract, with processors specifying delivery windows, quality/Brix standards, variety requirements, and plant destinations. Harvest timing is coordinated to match fruit maturity with plant capacity, minimizing delays between mechanical harvest and processing. Trucks may be provided by growers, independent agricultural haulers, or processor-affiliated logistics systems, depending on the contract structure and local relationships. During peak season, truck availability can become limiting factors because plants may receive very large volumes of tomatoes each day. Load-level grading is another important feature of tomato transportation logistics. According to interviews with UC Davis researchers, processing tomatoes are graded by load at delivery or receiving, with quality limits applied for mold, green fruit, worms, and other defects (K. Heeley, personal communication, May 20, 2026). Loads with high defect levels may be downgraded or rejected, which directly links hauling, harvest timing, and product quality. This creates a strong incentive to minimize delays between harvest and delivery, avoid excessive field hold times, and coordinate harvest with plant receiving capacity.

The cost of hauling is significant and has direct impacts on crop sourcing, contracting, and facility siting. Industry cost data for tomato paste production indicate that trucking represents a significant portion of the total cost: Morning Star's 2025 statistics estimate that trucking accounted for approximately 7.0% of 2024 industry-average tomato paste production cost (The Morning Star Company, 2025) . Transportation logistics also differ depending on whether the tomato stream is destined for paste, peeling, diced products, or other processed tomato lines (Hartz et al., 1999). Paste plants are designed for extremely high-throughput handling of mechanically harvested tomatoes and can receive large continuous flows during the season (Winans et al., 2019). Peeling and diced operations may have more specific fruit-quality requirements, because fruit integrity, color, tannins, and defect levels affect finished product quality. As a result, tomatoes routed to peeled or diced production face tighter constraints on harvest timing, bruising, and delivery delays than tomatoes routed to paste or puree (Arazuri et al., 2010). Product mix therefore affects not only by-product generation, but also the logistical requirements of the inbound crop. Because tomato hauling is seasonal, the system relies on temporary but highly coordinated transportation capacity. The main processing season generally runs from mid-summer into early fall, overlapping with other agricultural hauling demands in the Central Valley. This creates seasonal pressure on drivers, trailers, fuel, and plant receiving infrastructure. Efficient logistics require maintaining full trailer payloads, reducing plant wait times, scheduling harvest crews to avoid bottlenecks, and preventing fruit from sitting too long after harvest. Delays can reduce fruit quality, increase field or plant losses, and shift more material into off-spec or waste streams. Inbound hauling also affects the management of downstream by-products and wastewater. Since tomatoes arrive as a high-moisture crop, processors effectively import large volumes of water contained within the fruit. During processing, this water is released into product, wastewater, day during peak season must therefore coordinate crop intake with wastewater capacity, solids separation, discharge permits, and municipal or on-site treatment infrastructure. Overall, tomato hauling in the NSJV is best understood as an integrated field-to-factory logistics system rather than a simple commodity transport function. The economic viability of processing tomatoes depends on moving very large quantities of wet fruit over short time windows while preserving quality and matching plant capacity. Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Pomace Production and Supply

Tomato pomace is the main solid byproduct generated during industrial tomato processing. It is typically composed of tomato skins, seeds, fibrous pulp, residual soluble solids, and small amounts of entrained moisture-rich material separated during pulping, finishing, peeling, and related processing steps. Like other pomaces described in this report, tomato pomace is a wet, biologically active material generated at processing facilities during a compressed seasonal window. This makes its management highly dependent on moisture content, storage time, hauling distance, local outlet availability, and processor-specific handling infrastructure.

The amount and character of tomato pomace generated depends strongly on product mix. Paste production is the dominant processing pathway in the region and is generally the primary source of pomace, because skins, seeds, and fibrous solids are separated before or during concentration into paste. According to the UC Davis Byproduct Database, approximately 55% to 60% of processing tomatoes in handled in San Joaquin and Stanislaus counties are directed to paste, while nearly 85% of Merced County processing tomatoes are used for paste production (AI Institute for Next Generation Food Systems, n.d.). Peeling and diced tomato operations also generate wet residual streams, including peels, trim, slurry-like material, and wash-water solids, but these streams may differ from conventional paste pomace in moisture content, solids concentration, and downstream handling requirements.

Based on processor interviews, a reasonable order-of-magnitude estimate is that approximately 5% of inbound processing tomato tonnage is generated as pomace or comparable wet by-product material. As noted above, this yields a combined regional estimate of about 109,000 tons of wet pomace and comparable processing residuals in 2024. In practice, pomace generation varies by facility, tomato variety, fruit quality, product line, peeling technology, solids recovery efficiency, and whether processors classify certain wet residuals as pomace, slurry, green waste, wastewater solids, or compostable material.

To insulate themselves from these regulatory and operational risks, regional processors rely on a highly structured, localized byproduct market. The sales market for tomato pomace in the valley operates in two distinct ways: third-party brokers and direct sales. To protect themselves from a costly plant shutdown, mid-sized and independent processors typically rely on specialized agricultural brokers. These brokers handle the intense daily logistics, coordinating a steady stream of trucks to haul the perishable wet pomace straight to local dairies or independent drying facilities. In contrast, the industry's largest processing giants use their massive volume to bypass these entities entirely. By investing in their own onsite drying equipment, they can sell highly traceable, premium-grade pomace directly to global pet food brands and large-scale dairies. Thus, these large entities have significant impacts on the pricing and market entry for smaller or mid-sized operations. Historically, this has functioned as a cost-avoidance mechanism rather than a true revenue generator. The pomace market relies on the valley's massive dairy footprint to absorb the seasonal glut of high-moisture feed before it spoils. Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Animal Feed

The utilization of wet tomato pomace as livestock feed is the predominant byproduct use case in the North San Joaquin Valley, representing approximately 75% to 80% of the region's total pomace output. This high rate of adoption is driven by the close geographical alignment between major processing facilities and the dense cluster of dairy and beef operations across San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced counties. Because raw pomace leaves the cannery at roughly 80% moisture content, long-distance transport and long-term storage are impractical. Consequently, the material must be trucked immediately to nearby farms and integrated into cattle feed rations within a few days to prevent rapid fermentation and spoilage.

Tomato pomace functions as an economical feed ingredient, typically trading between $45 and $75 per ton on a delivered basis (Bell, 2018). However, because a processor's primary objective is to maintain continuous factory operations rather than maximize byproduct revenue, pricing fluctuates significantly during the peak harvest window in August. Pomace pricing is also exposed to broader feedstuff market dynamics including water availability (impacting availability of other crops like alfalfa and silage) and other crop prices (Bell, 2018). During these high-volume weeks, prices often drop to a bare cost-of-freight basis simply to ensure outbound trucks keep moving. Despite this price volatility, dairy nutritionists value the product for its dual-benefit nutritional profile; the skins provide a highly digestible source of fiber, while the seeds deliver approximately 20% crude protein on a dry-matter basis alongside beneficial natural fats (Nour et al., 2018).

In the broader regional feed market, tomato pomace competes directly with other widely available fibrous co-products, most notably almond hulls and corn silage. Historically, almond hulls have established the pricing baseline for local dairy fiber; when an abundant almond harvest oversupplies the market and depresses hull prices, the market value of tomato pomace decreases accordingly to remain competitive. However, emerging, alternative outlets are reducing the local availability of traditional dairy fiber, and tomato pomace is becoming an increasingly critical and predictable anchor for Central Valley livestock rations during the summer months.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Pet Food

The premium pet food sector represents the highest-value bulk application for tomato pomace, accounting for approximately 15% of the region's total output. National pet food manufacturers utilize dried tomato pomace as a functional ingredient, valuing it as a clean-label source of soluble fiber, Vitamin E, and lycopene for digestive and coat health. Premium, pet-food-grade dried tomato pomace commands a significant market premium compared to its wet livestock counterpart, at an estimated value of $500 and $700 per ton on a wholesale basis. This stark price difference reflects the value added through industrial processing, moisture stabilization, and rigorous safety compliance.

Pet food manufacturers require a shelf-stable ingredient with a moisture content under 10%, the material is highly concentrated; it takes approximately 5 tons of raw, wet pomace to produce a single ton of dried pomace.  Dehydration to a low moisture content is critical to ensure shelf stability and avoid spoilage during transport to pet food processing facilities. For pet-food applications, processors also must operate under animal-food safety systems that identify and control hazards such as Salmonella , often requiring validated process

<!-- image -->

controls or kill steps, together with sanitation controls to prevent recontamination (U.S. Food and Drug Administration, 2022).

Because of these intensive capital and operational requirements, the regional pet food channel is overwhelmingly dominated by industrial titans, most notably The Morning Star Packing Company. Morning Star has leveraged its unparalleled processing volume to justify the installation of onsite mechanical triple-pass drum dryers, solar-drying fields, and specialized extrusion lines, enabling them to market dried, shelf-stable pomace directly to global pet food brands (The Morning Star Company, n.d.). Crucially, their scale supports an integrated logistics infrastructure capable of transporting milled pomace in bulk via rail lines out of the Central Valley directly to major pet food manufacturing hubs across the Midwest. For smaller, independent processors in the North San Joaquin Valley, this creates a significant structural barrier. Lacking independent drying equipment and the volume required to secure bulk rail logistics, other regional canners cannot compete with Morning Star's pricing and market dominance, effectively excluding them from the premium pet food tier and keeping them tethered to the localized wet cattle feed market.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Extractives

At the highest tier of the byproduct value chain sits the extraction of specialized compounds, specifically lycopene from tomato skins and antioxidant-rich oils from the seeds. While these applications command premium prices in the cosmetic and functional food markets, they represent very small percentages of the total regional volume due to strict processing requirements. Like the pet food market, extraction requires the pomace to be dried immediately to preserve the active compounds before fermentation degrades them. Once dehydrated, the skins and seeds are mechanically separated; the skins undergo solvent or supercritical fluid extraction to isolate lycopene for use as a natural food colorant, while the seeds are cold-pressed into premium oils (Szabo et al., 2021). Because of the heavy infrastructure costs required to stabilize and process the material, this remains a niche in the valley, often operating via specialized contracts where dried material is shipped to dedicated chemical extraction facilities.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Land Application, Compost, and Anaerobic Digestion

For the remaining fraction of tomato pomace, processors rely on land application and composting as low-cost, emergency backup outlets. Direct land application as soil amendment is tightly restricted by the Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board under strict Waste Discharge Requirements (WDRs). Because wet pomace is highly acidic and ferments rapidly, it poses severe odor risks and attracts vinegar flies, requiring farm operators to disk the material into the soil immediately upon delivery. To avoid these regulatory challenges, some processors route excess pomace to commercial composting facilities, where it is blended with drier yard wastes to manage moisture and odor. The seasonality of tomatoes shapes how the industry interacts with bioenergy. Developing dedicated, on-site anaerobic digesters at the canneries is not technically or economically practical. Instead, some processors utilize a network of off-site regional digesters. Established municipal wastewater plants or large-scale dairy co-digesters across the valley accept tomato pomace on a periodic basis

during the summer surge. This arrangement benefits both parties: the processing plant safely unloads its excess organic waste, while the digester operators welcome the seasonal influx of high-sugar tomato material to temporarily boost their biogas production and renewable energy yields.The tomato processor would still incur a tipping fee in this case.
