content:
Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Seasonality, Stability, and Storage Constraints of Tomato Pomace

Tomato pomace and related processing residuals are generated almost entirely during the processing tomato harvest and canning season. In the North San Joaquin Valley, this season is concentrated from the summer to early fall, with major processing activity typically occurring from approximately July through October. During this period, processors receive very large daily volumes of wet tomatoes and generate correspondingly large volumes of pomace, mixed green waste, wastewater solids, and other organic residuals. This creates a short-duration biomass surge rather than a steady year-round feedstock supply. Any downstream user of tomato pomace must therefore be able to absorb large seasonal volumes or have infrastructure for stabilization, storage, or staged use.

The main storage constraint is the material's high moisture content and biological activity. Fresh tomato pomace contains skins, seeds, pulp, residual sugars, and entrained water, making it prone to rapid fermentation, odor generation, microbial growth, leachate formation, and quality deterioration if left unmanaged. Tomato pomace cannot be stockpiled outdoors for extended periods without creating nuisance, runoff, or permit-compliance issues. This limits the viability of long-term storage unless the material is dried, ensiled, blended into feed, composted, refrigerated, or otherwise stabilized soon after generation.

These stability constraints strongly shape market access. Wet pomace is best suited for nearby outlets that can receive and use the material quickly, such as local cattle feed users, composters, or other wet organic waste handlers. Higher-value markets, including pet food ingredients or specialty feed products, generally require drying or fractionation to create a more stable and transportable product. However, drying adds capital cost, energy demand, and market risk, particularly when regional supply increases and depresses prices. Overall, tomato pomace is a large and recurring feedstock, but its seasonality and instability mean that successful utilization depends less on annual tonnage alone and more on the availability of rapid handling, short-haul logistics, stabilization capacity, and permit-compliant residual management during the processing window.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Supply and Characteristics

Walnuts are an important specialty crop across the Northern San Joaquin Valley (NSJV), particularly in San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced counties, which together represent a significant share of California's walnut production. Over the period analyzed (2017-2024), these three counties produced between approximately 182,000 and 265,000 tons of in-shell walnuts annually, representing a substantial agricultural commodity stream within the region (Merced County, n.d.; San Joaquin County Agricultural Commissioner / Sealer of Weights & Measures, n.d.; Stanislaus County Agricultural Commissioner, n.d). Using average weight fractions of walnut fruit components, this corresponds to an estimated 405,000-588,000 tons of whole harvested fruit per year across the three counties combined.

On a field-weight basis, the walnut fruit consists of a fleshy green hull (or husk) surrounding a hard shell that encloses the edible kernel. Walnuts are typically harvested with the hull still attached. to hulling facilities. The hulling and cracking process separates the major walnut components in a manner broadly analogous to almond hulling and shelling, though the sequence differs due to the fruit's anatomy.

During cracking, mechanical crackers fracture the hard shell and release the edible kernels. A series of to grade kernels based on size, color, and integrity. Similar to almond processing, uncracked nuts or partially separated material may be recirculated through the cracking system to maximize kernel recovery.

Mechanical tree shakers dislodge the fruit, which is then swept and collected before being transported Following harvest, walnuts are transported to a hulling facility where the outer green hull is removed using mechanical hullers that peel away the fleshy husk from the shell. The hulled nuts are then washed to remove hull residues and dried with forced air to reduce moisture content and ensure safe and stable storage. After drying, walnuts may be stored in-shell or sent directly to cracking operations depending on market demand. California Walnut Board shipment statistics indicate that walnuts are marketed in both shelled and in-shell formats. Shipment data for recent marketing years show larger volumes of kernel shipments relative to in-shell shipments; when converted to in-shell equivalents using typical kernel recovery rates (~43%), these data suggest that roughly 60-70% of the crop is cracked for kernel production while the remainder is marketed in-shell (California Walnut Board, 2025c). vibrating screens, aspirators, and optical sorters are used to separate shell fragments from kernels and This process produces several material streams: the high-value kernel product, along with lower-value shell and hull coproducts. Hulls are typically separated early in the process at the hulling stage, while shells are generated during cracking. Together, these fractions represent the majority of the harvested walnut biomass.

County crop reports record walnut production in terms of hulled in-shell nut weight, meaning the mass of the green hull is not included in reported production statistics. To estimate total biomass associated with walnut production in the region, literature-based compositional fractions were applied to the reported in-shell tonnage. For the purposes of this analysis, walnut fruit was assumed to consist of approximately 45% in-shell nut and 55% green hull by total fruit weight, with the in-shell nut further divided into approximately 20% kernel and 25% shell relative to the whole fruit mass.

Shell residues available for industrial utilization were estimated assuming approximately 75% of walnuts are cracked for kernel production.

Applying these fractions to the reported production volumes indicates that walnut production in the three-county region generated approximately 223,000-323,000 tons of green hulls, 82,000-119,000 tons of kernels, and 100,000-146,000 tons of shells annually over the study period. While kernels represent the primary marketable product, hulls and shells together account for the majority of the harvested biomass and represent substantial agricultural residue streams with potential value for feed, bioenergy, and biomaterial applications.

content:
Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Walnut Hauling/Transportation

Transportation of harvested walnuts from orchards to hulling facilities represents an operationally important component of harvest logistics. After shaking and sweeping, walnuts are typically collected and loaded into field bins or bulk trailers and transported to a nearby huller where the green husk is removed and the nuts are dried to safe storage moisture levels. As with almonds, hauling distances are generally short because hulling infrastructure is geographically distributed across major walnut-producing regions of the Central Valley. In the Northern San Joaquin Valley (NSJV), growers in Merced, San Joaquin, and Stanislaus counties typically deliver walnuts to hulling facilities within a local service area, minimizing transportation costs and turnaround times during the compressed harvest window.

A key distinction between walnut and almond harvest logistics is the greater reliance on bin-based handling and intermediate drying infrastructure. Walnuts are often transported in wooden or plastic orchard bins rather than bulk trailers, particularly when harvest volumes are staged or when hulling facilities require controlled intake rates during peak harvest periods. After hulling and drying, walnuts are typically transferred in bulk to handlers or shelling facilities for storage, processing, and eventual marketing. This multi-step chain (illustrated above in figure 5-3) creates additional short-haul transportation movements within the regional supply chain compared with almonds. Walnut post-harvest handling typically involves two transportation stages: orchard-to-huller-dryer hauling, where hull removal and drying occur, followed by shipment of dried in-shell walnuts to handlers or shelling facilities for storage, processing, and marketing.

Hauling arrangements vary depending on the structure of the grower-handler relationship. Some growers transport walnuts themselves using farm-owned trucks or contracted seasonal drivers, while others rely on independent agricultural trucking companies that specialize in short-haul commodity transport during harvest. In many cases, handlers or cooperatives provide delivery allowances or embedded harvest service agreements that partially offset transportation costs, similar to cost-share hauling structures observed in the almond industry. These arrangements reflect the time-sensitive nature of walnut harvest: rapid transport to hulling facilities is important to prevent hull deterioration, mold development, or quality losses that could affect kernel value.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Walnut Hauling/Transportation

In many cases, handlers or cooperatives provide delivery allowances or embedded harvest service agreements that partially offset transportation costs, similar to cost-share hauling structures observed in the almond industry. These arrangements reflect the time-sensitive nature of walnut harvest: rapid transport to hulling facilities is important to prevent hull deterioration, mold development, or quality losses that could affect kernel value.

Commercial trucking rates for agricultural commodities in California typically range from approximately $4-6 per loaded truck-mile, which translates to roughly $0.17-$0.30 per ton-mile assuming payloads of about 20-24 tons per truck. At these rates, hauling costs remain modest when orchards are located within roughly 10-25 miles of a huller, which is common in the NSJV. As a result, transportation rarely dominates the economics of walnut handling, but it does influence facility siting and regional supply chains. Efficient logistics-such as minimizing wait times at hulling facilities, maintaining full payloads, and coordinating harvest schedules-are critical for keeping transportation costs predictable during peak harvest periods.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Hull Production and Supply

Walnut hulls, the green, fleshy outer pericarps of the fruit, are separated from the in-shell nut immediately during the post-harvest phase at specialized regional huller/dryer facilities. Because this separation occurs at the very beginning of the processing chain, before the nuts are dried and transferred to handlers, hull volume is not captured in standard county crop reports, which measure production strictly on a hulled, in-shell basis.

Applying standard post-harvest mass balance equations to the regional harvest data indicates that walnut production in San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced Counties generates an estimated 225,000 to 325,000 tons of wet hull material annually. This volume represents a front-loaded biomass surge that occurs over a compressed 6-to-8-week harvest window. The substantial tonnage is primarily a function of the hull's high moisture content, which typically ranges from 70% to 80% water at the time of processing. This high water weight makes the raw residue exceptionally heavy, dense, and physically distinct from the dry, stable shell coproduct generated later during cracking.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Hull Utilization and Market Structure

Unlike almond hulls, which represent a clean, sugar-dense commodity heavily utilized by the regional dairy sector, walnut hulls lack an established commercial market and generally function as an operational liability. The material is generally excluded from livestock feed and animal bedding channels due to its unique chemical profile. Walnut hulls contain high concentrations of astringent polyphenols and juglone Biochemical Constraint: Juglone Toxicity & Feed Exclusion concentrations of astringent polyphenols and juglone, an Unlike almond hulls, walnut hulls are excluded from livestock feed and bedding. They contain high allelopathic compound that is unpalatable to ruminants and toxic to horses. As a result, 75-85% of wet hulls are treated as a zero/negative-value disposal liability returned directly to orchard soils.

(5-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone), an allelopathic compound that is unpalatable to ruminants and highly toxic to horses.

Consequently, the market structure for walnut hulls is entirely disposal-driven and defined by a non-market allocation matrix:

- Direct Land Application (75% - 85%): The dominant pathway relies on hauling the wet hull slurry short distances to be broadcast onto fallow fields, pastures, or adjacent orchard soils using specialized manure spreaders. Because it is economically unfeasible to dry or pelletize this high-moisture slurry, the material must be returned to the soil as close to the huller as possible. The farm-gate value for this pathway is zero or negative, as the huller typically absorbs the localized hauling and spreading costs simply to clear facility volume.
- Commercial Co-Composting (10% - 15%): A secondary portion of the regional volume is diverted to centralized green-waste and municipal composting facilities. While raw hulls are difficult to compost in isolation due to their high organic acid content, commercial composters utilize the wet slurry as a valuable "moisture injection" to optimize the decomposition of excessively dry municipal yard trimmings and orchard wood chips. This pathway carries a negative farm-gate value, as hullers are typically subject to standard facility green-waste tipping fees.

Both primary disposal pathways are subject to strict regulatory oversight. As large stockpiles of wet hulls decompose, they generate highly acidic leachates capable of transferring concentrated nitrates and phytotoxic compounds into regional shallow groundwater basins. To mitigate these environmental risks, the California Regional Water Quality Control Boards mandate rapid, thin-layer field distribution, restricting the ability of handlers to store or accumulate the material over extended periods.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Alternative and Emerging Uses: Biosolarization and Extractives

To transition away from the regulatory and financial pressures of traditional land disposal, recent innovations focus on establishing alternative pathways. Both of these represent exploratory approaches that only handle a very small fraction of hull materials. Biosolarization leverages the volatile nature of the decomposing hull for natural pest management. Developed through cooperative efforts by the USDA Agricultural Research Service (ARS) and the University of California, Davis, the process involves mechanically incorporating crushed green hulls into pre-planted orchard soils (Hodson et al., 2022). Under the sealed, high-heat conditions achieved through plastic tarp coverings, the rapid anaerobic fermentation of the hull's organic compounds generates natural volatile fatty acids (Hodson et al., 2022). These compounds effectively strip oxygen from the soil matrix to eradicate destructive nematodes and soil-borne pathogens, providing growers with a value-in-kind offset against conventional chemical fumigant costs (Meshram et al., 2024). A second emerging, but niche, use is targeted extraction of high-value specialty compounds. The intrinsic juglone molecule functions as a robust, reddish-brown pigment classified as C.I. Natural Brown 7, drawing demand from the textile dyeing and natural cosmetic industries as a sustainable alternative to petroleum-derived synthetic dyes. Furthermore, due to an exceptionally high Total Phenolic Content (TPC), specialized chemical processors extract natural antioxidants and high-methoxy pectins from the walnut hulls for use as functional stabilizers and preservatives in pharmaceutical formulations. Unlike grape pigment extractives, which strictly need to avoid oxidation, biochemical extraction from walnut hulls requires a precisely managed window of initial atmospheric exposure to synthesize its primary target compounds. The active pigment and biocide, Precision Processing Window: 1 to 2 Hours Post-Harvest Active juglone pigments do not exist in living tissue; they are enzymatically converted from alpha-hydrojuglone within a narrow 1- to 2-hour post-harvest window. Processors must immediately arrest this cascade via flash dehydration or cryo-stabilization to prevent irreversible auto-oxidation and quality loss.

juglone, does not exist in living tissue but is enzymatically converted from its colorless precursor

(alpha-hydrojuglone) within a narrow one- to two-hour window post-harvest (Medic et al., 2022). If processors do not immediately arrest this chemical cascade at its peak concentration via flash dehydration or cryo-stabilization, these highly reactive molecules rapidly undergo irreversible auto-oxidation and cross-linking (Soto-Maldonado et al., 2019).

content:
Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Shell Production and Supply

Walnut shells are generated during cracking, after the green hull has already been removed and the dried in-shell nut has been transferred to a handler or shelling facility. Unlike walnut hulls, which are separated immediately after harvest and are generally wet, perishable, and locally managed, shells are produced later in the post-harvest chain and are comparatively dry, stable, and easier to store or transport. This makes shells the more durable and marketable walnut coproduct, although shell availability depends directly on the share of the crop that is cracked for kernel production rather than sold in-shell. By applying standard shell-to-kernel conversion factors, these data provide robust estimates of total shell volume generated annually in the region.

As described above, county crop reports record walnut production on a hulled in-shell basis, which excludes the green hull. Applying the chapter's assumed anatomical fractions indicates that walnut production in San Joaquin, Stanislaus, and Merced Counties generated approximately 100,000-146,000 tons of total shell material annually over the study period. However, not all of this material enters the shell-residue market in the year of production. Walnuts marketed in-shell retain the shell as part of the final food product, while walnuts cracked for kernel production generate shell residues at shelling facilities. Based on recent California Walnut Board shipment patterns and typical kernel recovery factors, roughly 60-70% of the crop is commonly cracked for kernel production, with the remainder marketed in-shell (~75,000-125,000 tons/yr).

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Shell Utilization and Market Structure

Public data on walnut shell utilization are substantially weaker than for almond hulls and shells. County crop reports provide walnut production values but generally do not report shell coproduct tonnage or prices as separate line items. Similarly, there is no publicly available walnut-shell equivalent to the almond industry's use estimates for shell bedding, bioenergy, soil amendment, and carryover. As a result, walnut shell utilization must be inferred from handler practices, commercial byproduct markets, and known end-use sectors rather than directly measured from county or statewide datasets.

While almond shells are relatively clean and uniform (making them easy for a sheller to sell directly to a dairy for bedding), walnut shells are generated at the cracker alongside "blower fluff" and "sorting room meal" (Abbattista et al., 2024). A raw load of walnut shells straight from the sheller contains residual nut meat, pellicle fragments, and internal pith (Abbattista et al., 2024). This organic "contamination" makes the shells unsuitable for high-value industrial use and can even cause molding issues if sold directly as bedding. For this reason, secondary processors and brokers like G3 Enterprises or Eco-Shell play critical roles in the byproduct valorization chain. They act as the "aggregator" that relieves the sheller of their bulk "raw" shell piles. These aggregators are the ones who 1) separate high-density shells from the 'blower fluff' , remove residual nut meats that would otherwise rot or mold, and sift the shells into precision mesh sizes required by the industrial applications (described below). Supply Chain Spread: Raw Shells vs. Graded Industrial Media Raw walnut shells straight from the cracker contain residual nut meats, pellicle fragments, and "blower fluff" that mold easily. Secondary aggregators buy raw loads for $30-$70/ton , clean out organic impurities, and precision-sift the dense shells into specific mesh sizes. This graded abrasive/filtration media sells for $900-$1,400/ton in bulk super-sacks.

The walnut shell market can be characterized as a tiered market structure rather than a single commodity channel. Lower-value, high-volume uses include biomass fuel, bedding, landscaping, mulch, and soil amendment. These outlets are geographically constrained and compete directly with almond shells, orchard wood chips, sawdust, rice hulls, and other regional lignocellulosic materials (many of which are described in other chapters). Higher-value uses require additional processing, including drying if needed, grinding, screening, dust control, and packaging. These uses include blasting and polishing media, filtration media, oil-field additives, carriers, fillers, and molded-product inputs.

The only major " market" where a walnut sheller might sell directly to an end-user is biomass energy. In the NSJV, some shellers have direct contracts with local cogeneration plants to ship their raw shells as fuel. However, as California's biomass plants have closed, even this "direct" outlet is increasingly managed by brokers who consolidate loads from multiple shellers to meet the high-tonnage requirements of the surviving plants.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Industrial Shell Products

Walnut shells support a distinct set of higher-value industrial markets. In these applications, shells are cleaned, ground, screened, and sold by particle size or performance specification rather than as undifferentiated bulk biomass. Common uses include abrasive blasting media, polishing and tumbling media, filtration media, drilling-fluid additives, fillers, carriers, and molded-product inputs. These markets take advantage of the shell's hardness, low density, biodegradability, and ability to be processed into consistent grades. Only the hardest, densest mid-sections of the shell meet the specifications for abrasive blasting and filtration. Industrial shell products differ from bulk shell outlets in three important ways. First, they require quality control. Shells must generally be free of excessive hull residue, soil, rocks, metal, mold, and other contaminants. Second, they require particle-size control. Different applications require different mesh sizes, dust levels, and flow properties. These are the particles that can survive the "attrition test" (remaining intact during high-pressure cycles). Because English walnut shells are thinner, the milling process inherently generates a higher percentage (often 50%+) of "flour" or "fines" (particles <200 μm), which are physically ineligible for the abrasive and filtration markets. This dictates the industrial use cases for walnut shells and also sets a ceiling for the fraction of shell residue that can be valorized in this way (typically 35-45%). Ground walnut shells have been a globally traded industrial commodity for decades, first documented with collaborations with the US Navy in the 1960s (Composition Materials Co., Inc., n.d.-b). They are the gold standard for "soft" abrasive blasting (used for cleaning engine parts, aerospace components, and delicate surfaces without pitting the underlying metal). The preservation of material integrity and primer and base coatings represents a major operational savings compared to other blasting agents (Composition Materials Co., Inc., n.d.-b). Moreover, they are environmentally degradable which provides a major advantage over mineral blasting agents. Another major industrial application of walnut shells is filtration media. Filtration media use cases are determined by the specific type of walnut being grown and the shell anatomy. Premium nutshell filters used in heavy industrial applications rely on black walnuts due to their durability, whereas English walnuts (the varietal grown in the NSJV) are instead used in commercial and industrial water treatment (Composition Materials Co., Inc., n.d.-a; G3 Enterprises, n.d.; Xedia Process Solutions, 2018). Due to the increased fragility of the English walnut shells, they are more suitable for single-pass and lower pressure applications ((Veolia Water Technologies, n.d.).

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Industrial Shell Products

Filtration media use cases are determined by the specific type of walnut being grown and the shell anatomy. Premium nutshell filters used in heavy industrial applications rely on black walnuts due to their durability, whereas English walnuts (the varietal grown in the NSJV) are instead used in commercial and industrial water treatment (Composition Materials Co., Inc., n.d.-a; G3 Enterprises, n.d.; Xedia Process Solutions, 2018). Due to the increased fragility of the English walnut shells, they are more suitable for single-pass and lower pressure applications ((Veolia Water Technologies, n.d.).

Both of these markets are mature, globally exported, and pays a premium compared to selling shells as generic filler, processors naturally divert as much high-quality, dry shell as possible to commercial grinding operations to meet this demand. Despite these high value applications, raw, unsifted shells straight from the cracker currently trade as a bulk commodity. Depending on the local contract with byproduct brokers like G3 Enterprises, raw shells generally fetch between $30 and $70 per ton, consistent with regional waste disposal prices. In seasons with high supply and low biomass demand, this price can drop to "cost of removal" levels, where the huller essentially gives the shells away to avoid stockpile regulations. Once the shells are transported to a secondary processor (like Eco-Shell), they are cleaned of residual meat/pith and milled into specific mesh sizes. This graded media retails for $900 to $1,400 per ton when purchased in bulk "super-sacks" (2,000 lbs). While there is significant value spread between the acquired cost of the shell feedstock and product value, numerous cost and energy intensive steps must take place including transportation, precision milling (to specific sieve/mesh sizes), sifting/grading, and packaging (Petro Naft, 2026).

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Bioenergy

Walnut shells are well suited to bioenergy applications because of their low moisture after drying and relatively high heating value. Published biomass datasets report walnut shell lower heating values around 19 MJ/kg, while recent combustion testing found pelletized walnut shell fuel values in the range of roughly 16.9 MJ/kg with low moisture and ash contents under tested conditions (Nabiałczyk et al., 2025).

However, bioenergy markets are constrained by the same factors discussed in the almond chapter: biomass power generation has declined in competitiveness relative to lower-cost renewable electricity sources, and the economics of combustion or gasification are highly sensitive to delivered fuel cost, facility proximity, power-purchase terms, and the ability to use process heat. As a result, bioenergy is likely to remain an important but limited and declining outlet for walnut shells.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Biochar

The rapid emergence of biochar as a viable destination for walnut shells is a direct response to a mounting disposal crisis in California's agricultural sector. For decades, traditional biomass cogeneration plants served as the primary relief valve for the industry's bulk shells, but a steady wave of facility closures (as described above) has dramatically reduced this use pathway. In its place, pyrolysis, the thermal decomposition of organic material in an anoxic environment, has transformed from an experimental waste-management strategy into a policy-supported priority. This shift away from traditional open combustion is strongly supported by state and federal regulatory frameworks aimed at soil carbon enhancement. For instance, the California Department of Food and Agriculture (CDFA) Healthy Soils Program and the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), under Conservation Practice Standard 384 and Code 336 (Soil Carbon Amendment), provide structured financial assistance to encourage the land application of stable carbon materials. These frameworks have shifted the baseline economics of agricultural byproducts, prompting broader industry initiatives to integrate carbon-stabilizing practices directly into regional orchard management systems This institutional alignment was prominently highlighted by the California Walnut Board's "Growing with Biochar" initiatives, which directly train regional growers on integrating these thermal conversion systems into local orchard management (California Walnut Board, 2025b).

From a material standpoint, the high lignin content and density of walnut shells make them an ideal feedstock for thermochemical conversion, delivering a high yield of fixed carbon compared to less dense agricultural residues. Thermochemical processing stabilizes the volatile fractions of the biomass, yielding a highly porous, long-lived biocarbon or biochar. When applied agronomically, this material alters the physical properties of local soils by improving aggregate stability, optimizing water-holding capacity, and creating structural matrices that enhance nutrient retention (Gao et al., 2025; Nisa & Bhaduri, 2024; Parikh et al., 2017). Beyond localized soil-health benefits, the market for this material is increasingly driven by the monetization of certified Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) credits. By certifying the net carbon sequestered through protocols approved by international registries, secondary processors can translate a volume-heavy material handling liability into a verified carbon removal asset.

This transition from legacy bulk disposal to advanced thermochemical processing is actively reshaping the shell landscape of the North San Joaquin Valley. In locations like Escalon (San Joaquin County), vertically integrated operations have integrated on-site thermal conversion systems directly into their processing complexes (Loria, 2026). These configurations allow operators to process bulk shell residues immediately post-cracking, capturing the generated syngas or thermal energy to offset facility operational utility costs while simultaneously producing a uniform, stabilized carbon product for regional agricultural markets. This commercial deployment is closely mirrored by public-sector research initiatives. Multi-year cooperative projects between the USDA Agricultural Research Service (ARS) in Albany and the University of California, Davis, continue to analyze various thermal treatment envelopes, including pyrolysis, gasification, and torrefaction, to optimize pore distribution and surface area.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Filler, Bedding, and Mulch

The baseline tier of the walnut shell market consists of residual fillers, ground flours, and un-milled agricultural residues that fail to meet the rigorous purity, structural density, or particle-size specifications required for filtration and abrasive blasting. This category captures the highly fractured shell fragments, internal pith, and pellicle "fluff" generated during primary cracking, as well as the fine flour inevitably produced during secondary milling operations. Because these materials lack the mechanical resilience needed to survive high-pressure industrial applications, they are sold at a substantial discount compared to graded media, serving instead as inexpensive functional extenders in industrial adhesives, rubber compounds, household cleansers, and plastic composites (Barczewski et al., 2017).

The marketing of these lower-tier fillers is shared between both ends of the processing chain. Secondary processors, who deliberately "mine" the shell stream for premium shell fractions, market the resulting fine-milled flour to chemical and manufacturing sectors as a strategy to maximize total tonnage utilization and recoup costs from milling losses (Barczewski et al., 2017). Concurrently, primary shell handling/shelling facilities and specialized byproduct brokers like G3 Enterprises directly market the coarser, un-milled "blower fluff" and sorting-room fractions to regional buyers for livestock bedding, landscaping mulch, and low-grade structural fillers, operating primarily to clear physical volume from handling facilities (G3 Enterprises, n.d.; ( Pelletized tree nut animal litter and method of making same , 2017).

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Seasonality, Stability, and Storage Constraints of Byproduct Streams

Walnut shell generation is seasonal but less temporally concentrated than hull generation because cracking may occur after drying and storage rather than immediately at harvest. Walnut harvest and hulling are concentrated in the fall, but dried in-shell walnuts can be stored and cracked over a longer period in response to market demand, handler capacity, and shipment schedules. This creates a more distributed shell-generation profile than the immediate harvest-driven surge associated with walnut hulls. California Walnut Board inventory reports show substantial in-shell and shelled walnut inventories remaining several months into the marketing year; for example, as of March 31, 2025, the 2024/25 crop still had approximately 201 million pounds of in-shell inventory and 144 million pounds of shelled inventory (California Walnut Board, 2025a). This indicates that walnuts move through storage, cracking, and shipment channels over time rather than being cracked immediately after harvest.

Once generated, walnut shells are comparatively stable. Their low moisture content and lignocellulosic composition allow them to be stored outdoors or under cover for extended periods with limited biological degradation, provided they are protected from excessive moisture accumulation, soil contamination, and compaction. Storage requirements are therefore less stringent than for walnut hulls, which are wet and prone to microbial activity. However, storage conditions still matter for higher-value uses. Shells destined for abrasion, filtration, drilling additives, cosmetics, or molded products require cleaner handling, tighter particle-size control, and lower contamination than shells used for bulk fuel or bedding. For these uses, processors may need to segregate shell material, minimize fines or foreign material, and maintain traceable lots.

Woody biomass handling (from almond, olive, and walnut orchards and vineyards) has dramatically changed in the past 5 years as a result of final implementation of agricultural burn bans. Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Woody Biomass from Orchard and Vineyard Systems: Overview

Woody biomass from orchard and vineyard systems represents a substantial and structurally distinct component of the agricultural residue stream in the North San Joaquin Valley. Generated through orchard and vineyard removals, annual pruning, and thinnings, this material consists primarily of lignocellulosic wood fractions that differ fundamentally from other agricultural byproducts such as almond hulls or fruit pomace. While large in volume (> 1,000,000 tons/yr), woody biomass is characterized by low bulk density, spatial distribution, and limited intrinsic market value. These properties make it difficult to transport and aggregate, shaping a system in which management decisions are driven more by cost and logistics than by biomass value.

Unlike other agricultural byproduct systems in the region, the handling of woody biomass in the NSJV is governed primarily by policy and regulatory constraints, particularly the phase-out of open agricultural burning. As a result, growers must actively manage biomass through grinding, soil incorporation, or limited off-site utilization pathways. This has led to the rapid adoption of practices such as whole orchard recycling (WOR), as well as growing interest in alternative uses including bioenergy, biochar, and fiber-based materials. However, the feasibility of these pathways remains tightly constrained by transportation costs, storage limitations, and the seasonal and spatial variability of biomass supply. This chapter examines the generation, handling, economics, and emerging opportunities for woody biomass across almond, walnut, vineyard, and olive systems in the NSJV.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Policy and Regulatory Drivers

The management of woody biomass from orchard and vineyard systems in the North San Joaquin Valley is fundamentally shaped by air quality regulations governing agricultural burning. Unlike other agricultural byproducts that are primarily influenced by market demand, woody biomass disposal practices are largely policy-driven, reflecting the region's long-standing air quality challenges.

The San Joaquin Valley is designated as a non-attainment area for federal and state standards for particulate matter (PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀) and ozone (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2024). Historically, open burning of agricultural residues (e.g. orchard removals, vineyard prunings, crop residues) was a widespread and cost-effective disposal method. However, these practices contributed significantly to regional air pollution, prompting a multi-decade regulatory effort to phase out agricultural burning.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > State Legislative Framework (SB 705)

In 2003, California enacted Senate Bill 705 (SB 705), which established a statewide mandate to phase out open agricultural burning in the San Joaquin Valley (California Air Resources Board, n.d.). The legislation required a gradual elimination of burning across crop categories, while allowing for temporary postponements where:

- No economically feasible alternatives existed,
- Sufficient funding for alternatives was not available, and
- California Air Resources Board (CARB) concurred with such determinations.

Over time, these postponements enabled a phased transition as new technologies, practices, and funding mechanisms emerged. Subsequent regulatory actions and updates have progressively tightened restrictions, culminating in a near-complete prohibition on open burning for most agricultural materials.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > District Rule 4103 and Implementation

At the regional level, SB 705 is implemented through San Joaquin Valley Air Pollution Control District Rule 4103 (Open Burning), which establishes the framework for regulating agricultural burning (San Joaquin Valley Air Pollution Control District, n.d.-b).

Under Rule 4103:

- Open burning of most agricultural materials, including orchard removals, vineyard removals, and prunings, is prohibited.
- Limited exceptions remain for specific cases such as diseased materials or situations where no feasible alternatives exist.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Regulatory Mandate: The Phase-Out of Agricultural Burning

Under California Senate Bill 705 and San Joaquin Valley APCD Rule 4103, open agricultural burning of orchard removals, vineyard removals, and surface-harvested prunings is prohibited as of January 1, 2025 . This policy shift transforms woody biomass from a low-cost disposal stream into an actively managed, policy-driven handling requirement across all perennial crops

- A Smoke Management System governs any remaining permitted burning to minimize air quality impacts.

The Air Pollution Control District is required to review agricultural burning practices every five years and make updated recommendations based on technological feasibility, economic considerations, and environmental impacts. The 2024 San Joaquin Valley Agricultural Burning Report documents that the region has achieved a near-complete phase-out of agricultural burning for the majority of crop types, including woody biomass from orchards and vineyards ((San Joaquin Valley Air Pollution Control District, 2024).

Recent regulatory updates have accelerated the transition away from burning. As of January 1, 2025, open burning of orchard removals, vineyard removals, and surface-harvested prunings are effectively prohibited across the region, with only narrow exceptions remaining.

<!-- image -->

2024 value represents tons burned to date

Figure 6-1. Agricultural burns in the San Joaquin Valley (by tons) since 2000 (San Joaquin Valley Air Pollution Control District, 2024).

This transition represents a significant structural shift in biomass management:

- Historically dominant practices (open burning) have been largely eliminated.
- Alternative practices, such as grinding, chipping, soil incorporation, and limited off-site utilization, have become the primary pathways.
- Remaining burn allowances are restricted to specific cases (e.g., diseased material, certain crop types with limited alternatives).

The report also highlights that the phase-out applies broadly across perennial cropping systems, including almonds, walnuts, vineyards, and olives, making it a system-wide driver rather than crop-specific regulation.

State funding has played a critical role in scaling these alternatives. For example, California allocated substantial funding (e.g., ~$180 million in 2021) to support the transition away from agricultural burning and enable adoption of alternative practices (California Air Resources Board, 2021).

These programs effectively transform biomass management from a purely cost burden into a partially subsidized system, enabling practices such as WOR to reach cost parity with historical burning in many cases.

A key structural feature of current incentive programs is that payments are typically provided on a per-acre basis, while the costs of biomass processing scale more directly with the volume of material generated (i.e., tons per acre). This creates meaningful variation across crops. For example, walnut orchards, which Economic Disparity: Per-Acre Grants vs. High-Biomass Crops Because incentive programs pay on a per-acre basis , higher-density crops receive a much lower subsidy per ton of biomass. Walnut removals generate 80-120 tons per acre compared to 30-65 tons per acre for almonds. The larger tree trunks and higher density increase grinding costs, leaving walnut growers with a significantly smaller relative cost offset.

generate substantially higher biomass per acre than almonds, receive similar per-acre incentive payments, resulting in a lower effective subsidy on a per-ton basis. At the same time, walnut removals often incur higher processing costs due to larger tree size and wood density. As a result, incentive programs may provide a smaller relative cost offset for higher-biomass systems, potentially affecting adoption dynamics across crop types.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Implications for Woody Biomass Systems

The regulatory phase-out of agricultural burning has fundamentally reshaped the woody biomass system in the NSJV:

- From disposal to management: Growers must now actively manage biomass through grinding, incorporation, or transport rather than relying on low-cost burning.

- Policy-driven adoption of alternatives: Practices such as WOR have scaled rapidly not because of intrinsic market value, but due to regulatory mandates and incentive support.
- Creation of new supply streams: The elimination of burning has increased the potential of woody biomass for emerging utilization pathways (e.g. biochar, materials), although these markets remain limited.
- Persistent economic constraints: Despite incentives, biomass handling remains a net cost in most cases, reinforcing the importance of logistics, proximity to outlets, and continued policy support.

Overall, policy and regulatory drivers, particularly the phase-out of agricultural burning, are the primary force shaping the generation, handling, and potential utilization of woody biomass across orchard and vineyard systems in the region.

Bioenergy and cogeneration remain established but declining pathways. While woody biomass can be used effectively as a combustion fuel due to its relatively high calorific value, the number of operational biomass power facilities in California has decreased over time, and remaining facilities are highly capacity-constrained and geographically limited. content:
Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Woody Biomass Hauling/Transportation

Transportation is the single most important logistical constraint on woody biomass utilization. The material's low bulk density and high volume-to-mass ratio mean that trucks often reach volumetric capacity before weight limits, reducing payload efficiency relative to denser commodities. Even when fully loaded, hauling costs can quickly exceed the delivered value of the material.

Hauling costs typically fall in the range of $0.17-$0.30 per ton-mile, assuming full truckloads of 20-24 tons and efficient turnaround times (Duncan et al., 2024). Because transportation costs scale linearly with distance while material value remains low or negative, even modest increases in haul distance can render otherwise viable utilization pathways uneconomic.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > As a result:

- Economical transport distances are limited, typically to <20-40 miles for most use cases.
- Biomass power plants, composting facilities, or other end-use sites must be located in close proximity to generation areas to be viable.
- In many cases, transporting biomass off-site is more expensive than processing it in-field, even when off-site utilization pathways exist.

These constraints explain why the majority of woody biomass remains within or near the originating field, rather than entering broader regional or state-level markets.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > System Overview

Orchard removals represent the largest source of woody biomass in perennial agricultural systems in the NSJV. These removals occur at the end of an orchard's productive life, typically every 20-25 years for almonds and somewhat longer for other tree crops, and generate substantial quantities of lignocellulosic material in a short time frame.

Removal operations typically involve pushing over trees, followed by grinding or chipping in-field. The resulting material may be incorporated into the soil, left as surface mulch, or transported off-site depending on local conditions, economics, and regulatory constraints.

Biomass yields from removals are significant. For almonds, removal volumes are typically on the order of 30 to 65 tons per acre, with additional contributions from prunings and other woody residues over the orchard lifecycle. Across the NSJV, this translates to between 775,000 - 1,600,000 tons of woody biomass annually, depending on yields and orchard turnover rates.

Figure 6-4. Estimated whole biomass removal volumes from major biomass sources explored in this report.

<!-- image -->

Today, WOR, the process of grinding trees and incorporating the biomass into the soil, has emerged as the dominant pathway in many parts of the region. Industry estimates suggest that WOR now accounts for a majority of orchard removal acreage in almonds, with adoption continuing to increase as regulatory pressure intensifies and incentive programs offset costs.

Economically, orchard removal is a cost-driven system. Unlike almond hulls or shells, which are established commodities with stable end markets, woody biomass from removals has limited intrinsic market value. As a result, management decisions are primarily determined by:

- cost of removal and processing,
- availability of incentives,
- proximity to alternative outlets (e.g., biomass facilities, compost facilities), and
- regulatory constraints on disposal.

With incentives applied, WOR can approach cost parity with historical push-and-burn practices, particularly when long-term soil health benefits are considered.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Almonds

Almond orchards are the dominant source of woody biomass in the NSJV due to their large acreage base and relatively high turnover rates. Removal yields are typically 30-65 tons per acre, making almonds one of the most significant contributors to regional biomass supply (Almond Board of per year across the three counties, with typical years around 19,000-20,000 acres per year (Almond Board of California, n.d.-b). On an annual basis, total almond biomass from orchard removals is

California, n.d.-a). In recent years, total acreage removed has ranged between 13,000 and 30,000 acres expected to be 570,000 - 1,230,000 tons/yr. Adoption of whole orchard recycling is particularly advanced in almonds, supported by both incentive programs and extensive research demonstrating benefits to soil organic matter, water retention, and long-term productivity. Recent estimates indicate that a substantial share of almond removals, on the order of 50% or more, now utilize WOR practices.

Post-harvest removals usually begin immediately after the fall harvest (Late October-January). Growers aim to have trees pulled and ground by late January to prepare the land for spring planting or to complete WOR before the rainy season makes soil work difficult.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Walnuts

Walnut orchards generally produce larger individual trees with higher per-tree biomass compared to almonds, which can increase total biomass per acre (80-120 tons/acre) and affect grinding and handling requirements (Reyes, 2024). Walnut orchard turnover rates tend to be lower (~33 year orchard life), resulting in less frequent but potentially more logistically intensive removal events compared to almonds (University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, n.d.). In recent years, a combination of increased input costs (namely fertilizer), varietal trends, and water pressures have increased turnover rates. Assuming a 4.5% annual removal rate, this results in between 394,000 and 592,000 tons of biomass/yr. The higher wood density and trunk size may increase grinding costs and equipment requirements

relative to almonds, but overall management pathways, particularly the use of in-field processing and soil incorporation, are similar. However, because incentive programs such as the Ag Burn Alternatives Grant Program are structured on a per-acre basis, walnut systems receive a lower effective subsidy on a per-ton basis compared to almonds. At the same time, higher biomass volumes and larger trunk sizes can increase grinding and handling costs, resulting in a smaller relative cost offset and potentially making whole orchard recycling less economically attractive for walnut removals relative to almond systems. Similar to almonds, walnut removals follow the late-fall harvest (November-February). Because walnuts are often planted in heavier soils in the NSJV, contractors prioritize the early winter months

(November/December) before peak winter rains saturate the ground and impede heavy equipment.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Olives

Olive orchards produce denser, more lignified wood compared to almonds, which can influence grinding efficiency and decomposition rates when incorporated into soil. Orchard spacing and tree architecture also differ, affecting both biomass distribution and removal logistics. For the olive sector, a removal rate of 2.5% to 3.0% is assumed, reflecting a replacement cycle on the order of ~25-40 years depending on orchard type as newer super-high density (SHD) oil systems typically have shorter productive lifespans (Takeoka et al., 2021). This rate accounts for the gradual phase-out of older, traditional table-olive groves in the NSJV while acknowledging that the region's newer, high-density oil plantings remain in their prime productive years. Applying this rate to the 7,189 bearing acres yields approximately 180 to 215 acres of removals annually, depending on orchard density (15-25 tons/acre), this generates a modest biomass stream ranging from roughly 2,700 to 5,400 dry tons per year (San Joaquin Valley Air Pollution Control District, 2020). As these "first-generation" SHD orchards (planted in the late 2000s and early 2010s) reach their 20-year limit, the annual removal rate in the NSJV is likely to rise from the current 2.5-3.0% to a more aggressive 4.0-5.0%, mirroring the turnover seen in nut crops.

Olive removals often trend slightly later than deciduous crops because olives are evergreens (January - April). Removal usually occurs in late winter or early spring once the harvest is finalized and the grower has confirmed the replacement or land schedule for the new year.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Vineyards

Vineyard removals differ substantially from tree crops in both scale and structure. Grapevines generate significantly lower biomass per acre than orchard trees, but removals occur more frequently due to shorter vineyard lifespans.

Based on the regional footprint of 102,807 bearing acres, the wine grape sector is undergoing significant changes. Industry trends through 2024-2026 indicate an aggressive removal rate of approximately 7.0% as the market adjusts following several years of oversupply (Lodi Winegrape Commission, 2025). This results in the projected removal of roughly 7,200 acres annually. Due to the lower woody mass of vine cordons compared to tree crops, estimated biomass density ranges from 4 to 8 dry tons per acre, generating a total annual stream of 29,000 to 58,000 dry tons (San Joaquin Valley Air Pollution Control District, 2021).

Removal operations typically involve pulling vines and trellising systems, followed by chipping or piling. Because of the lower biomass volume and dispersed nature of vineyard removals, in-field incorporation or localized disposal is often preferred over hauling to centralized facilities.

Vineyard removals are strictly dormant-season activities (October-February). There is significant pressure to complete these by early March before bud break.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > System Overview

In addition to the biomass generated from orchard removals and land-use transitions, the NSJV produces a significant annual volume of woody residues through standard maintenance pruning. Based on the standing acreage (total bearing acres minus annual removals), these residues represent a renewable biomass stream that is primarily managed on-site. Across the four major streams, prunings, thinnings, and annual removals amount to 440,000 - 700,000 tons of biomass per year.

Figure 6-5. Estimated annual thinning and pruning volumes from major biomass sources explored in this report.

<!-- image -->

Table 6-3. Management practices for woody biomass derived from annual thinning and pruning activities.

|-----------------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| In-Field Mulching     | ~90%-95%                | The most common fate. Prunings are shredded in-place using flail mowers and incorporated into the soil surface. This practice supports soil organic matter (SOM) and moisture retention.                                  |
| Bioenergy Feedstock   | <5%                     | Minimal. Due to low bulk density and high collection/transportation costs, pruning "fine wood" is rarely exported to biomass power plants unless part of a larger whole-tree removal project.                             |
| On-Site Composting    | Minimal, but increasing | Facilitated by recent legislation (e.g., SB 279), growers are increasingly permitted to compost larger volumes of agricultural waste on-site, combining prunings with other organic materials to produce soil amendments. |

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Almonds

Almond prunings and thinnings represent the largest recurring biomass flux in the region, primarily generated through mechanical hedging, topping, and the structural training of younger trees. Based on a standing footprint of 500,000 acres and a specific yield estimate of 0.64 to 0.96 dry tons per acre, the almond sector contributes between 305,000 and 460,000 dry tons of annual pruning biomass (Aliaño-González et al., 2022). While thinnings in early years establish orchard structure, mature maintenance focuses on light penetration. Under current regional standards, this material is almost exclusively shredded in-place to support soil organic matter. These activities are concentrated in the dormant season, typically occurring from December through February, though light structural thinnings of young trees may occur periodically through the spring.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Walnuts

Mechanical hedging and topping remain the regional standard. Walnut pruning and thinning residues are generally somewhat higher than almonds due to larger tree size, typically on the order of ~0.75 to 1.25 dry tons per acre annually (Aliaño-González et al., 2022). With a standing footprint of approximately 109,591 acres, walnuts contribute the largest share of pruning biomass, totaling 78,000 - 131,000 dry tons annually. Major pruning operations generally take place in late winter (February to March) before the sap begins to flow, though some growers increasingly utilize summer pruning in July and August to minimize disease risk and manage vigorous crown growth.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Olives

Pruning intensity in olives is often higher in Super High Density (SHD) oil orchards to maintain machine-harvesting 'clearance'. For the 7,189 standing acres, a yield of 0.60 to 1.50 dry tons per acre results in a projected 4,200 - 10,000 dry tons (Tittmann et al., 2013). To avoid frost damage and water-borne diseases like olive knot, the primary pruning window occurs in the spring, typically between February and May, with light maintenance thinnings often following in the summer months.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Vineyards

Vineyard prunings consist of dormant canes removed to manage crop load and vine architecture. From the 102,807 standing acres, a yield of 0.50 to 1.00 dry tons per acre generates an annual stream of 48,000 to 96,000 dry tons (Tittmann et al., 2013). The bulk of this woody material is generated during the primary pruning window of January through early March, though secondary green thinnings and canopy "leaf pulling" occur throughout the summer growing season to improve fruit quality.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Economics and Logistics

The economics of woody biomass in the NSJV are fundamentally defined by three characteristics: low bulk density, spatial dispersion, and limited market value. Therefore, the regional management is motivated to minimize costs to orchards under regulatory constraints rather than generating additional revenues. Unlike almond hulls or shells, which benefit from centralized processing and stable commodity markets, woody biomass must generally be managed near the point of generation to remain economically viable. Woody biomass in the NSJV is not constrained by supply, but by the cost of aggregating, transporting, and temporally aligning that supply with demand.

The total cost of managing woody biomass varies by crop, orchard/vineyard age, and chosen pathway, but is generally composed of three primary components:

- ●
- Removal and processing ($/acre): Includes pushing, grinding, and/or chipping of trees or vines. For orchard removals, this represents the largest single cost component and can exceed $1,000 per acre depending on tree size and site conditions (Zuber, personal communication, October 30, 2025).
- ●
- Grinding and size reduction ($/ton): Biomass must typically be chipped or ground before transport or incorporation. Costs scale with material size, density, and contamination (e.g., soil content from root balls). Grinding and size reduction can range between $25-$50/ton, with higher values in challenging configurations such as vineyards (Duncan et al., 2024).

Hauling costs typically fall in the range of $0.17-$0.30 per ton-mile, assuming full truckloads of 20-24 tons and efficient turnaround times (Tittmann et al., 2013). These costs increase rapidly with distance and often represent the limiting factor in determining whether off-site utilization

- Transportation ($/ton-mile): is viable.

Because woody biomass has limited market value, often near zero or even negative when disposal fees are included, these costs are rarely offset by revenues. Growers typically select the lowest-cost compliant pathway, making regional incentive programs the primary driver for adopting higher-cost alternatives like WOR.

In this cost-driven system, incentive programs play a critical role in shaping behavior. Programs such as the Ag Burn Alternatives Grant Program, Healthy Soils Program, and Conservation Stewardship Program offset the incremental costs of grinding, incorporation, and other alternatives to burning. In many cases, these incentives enable WOR to reach near cost parity with historical push-and-burn practices (Zuber, personal communication, October 30, 2025). Additionally, these programs provide the near-immediate cash flow necessary to pay grinding contractors, making it a more viable short-term business decision turning a long-term agronomic experiment into a viable short-term business decision.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Without these incentives:

- In-field incorporation would often remain more expensive than burning (where permitted),
- Off-site utilization pathways would be even less competitive, and
- Adoption of alternative practices would likely be significantly lower.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Seasonality, Stability, and Storage Constraints of Byproduct Streams

Storage presents an additional challenge that further limits the development of valorization markets.

The supply of woody biomass in the NSJV is both spatially distributed and seasonally concentrated:

- Supply Peaks: Biomass generation creates a "winter surge", from November to March. Orchard and vineyard removals generate massive volumes during discrete dormant-season events, while prunings provide smaller, distributed annual flows, but at a small fraction compared to the dormant season activities.
- Market Misalignment: This irregular supply profile makes it difficult to aggregate material at a scale that matches the steady, year-round demand required by industrial bioenergy or manufacturing facilities.

Woody biomass from removals and prunings present several challenges to be stored economically:

- High volume and low density require large storage footprints.

- Irregular particle size and contamination (e.g., soil, rocks) complicate handling and reduce uniformity.
- Moisture variability can affect material quality, particularly for combustion or higher-value applications.
- Large piles of chipped material may pose fire risk or biological degradation concerns over time.

Taken together, these factors make long-term storage economically unattractive, reinforcing a system in which biomass is either utilized immediately or managed in-field.

Regional Biomass Valorization and Byproduct Market Assessment - Full Report > Alternative and Emerging Uses

Despite the structural constraints outlined above, woody biomass from orchard and vineyard systems presents several emerging opportunities for higher-value utilization. These pathways are largely motivated by the need to create local or semi-local demand that can overcome transportation and storage limitations, rather than relying on long-distance commodity markets. As a result, most viable alternatives are those that can either be deployed near the point of generation or significantly increase the value density of the material.

One of the most prominent emerging pathways is biochar production, in which woody biomass is thermochemically converted into a stable, carbon-rich solid that can be applied to soils. Biochar offers dual benefits: it provides agronomic value through improved soil structure, water retention, and nutrient holding capacity, while also enabling long-term carbon sequestration. Compared to many other emerging biomass utilization pathways, biochar production is a relatively mature and commercially demonstrated technology, with established conversion systems and a growing base of operational projects. As a result, the primary barriers to scale are less related to technical feasibility and more to feedstock logistics, capital deployment, and the development of stable end markets (e.g., carbon credits and agronomic demand).

Programs within California's carbon market framework, along with emerging voluntary carbon market methodologies, are beginning to create monetizable credits for avoided emissions and durable carbon storage from biomass utilization pathways (California Air Resources Board, 2023). Several biochar projects are actively operating in California and generating carbon credits through voluntary carbon markets (e.g., Puro.earth, Carbonfuture). While these credits are not currently part of California's compliance offset program, they represent an emerging revenue stream tied to durable carbon removal that may improve the economics of woody biomass utilization. These incentives can partially offset the costs of biomass collection and processing, improving the economic viability of biochar systems relative to traditional disposal pathways. However, like other uses, biochar deployment remains constrained by the need for distributed processing infrastructure or efficient aggregation within limited transport distances.

Beyond biochar, woody biomass is being explored as a feedstock for engineered wood products, fiber-based materials, and biocomposites, where its lignocellulosic structure can be utilized in applications such as particleboard, molded fiber products, and biodegradable packaging. These applications offer the potential for higher unit value than energy uses, but they require consistent material quality, preprocessing, and reliable supply chains, which are difficult to achieve given the fragmented and seasonal nature of biomass generation in the NSJV. Similarly, biomass can be used in composting systems or as a bulking agent in organic waste processing, though these uses are generally

Overall, the viability of alternative and emerging uses depends less on the technical feasibility of conversion and more on the ability to align feedstock supply with processing infrastructure in space and time. Pathways that can densify material, operate at distributed scales, or generate additional value through environmental credits (e.g., carbon sequestration) are the most promising. However, emerging uses are likely to remain niche or location-specific rather than forming large-scale, region-wide markets.

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > Abstract

The XRF analyzer enables rapid screening of elemental composition in raw biomass samples, ranging from light elements to heavier metals. This procedure is designed to ensure the safe operation of the Vanta Max handheld X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer by clearly outlining the essential operating steps and the critical safety controls required to protect the operator.

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > PPE

- Long Pants
- Closed-toed shoes ■
- Safety glasses - must be worn at all times in the lab space
- Lab coat - must be worn when spending extended time in the lab space or any time when doing hands-on work in the lab
- Latex or Nitrile Gloves - must be worn anytime when doing hands-on work in the lab ■
- A whole-body badge (OSL dosimeter) is required to be clipped to the outside of your labcoat on the upper torso (between chest and waist area) facing outward to the radiation source
- Extremity rings are required to be worn on your fingers underneath the nitrile gloves, facing outward to the radiation source. ■

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > Ergonomics

Lift heavy objects (work station weighs ~22lb when it is loaded with Vanta XRF analyzer and battery installed) with proper form - Get as close to the load as possible. Keep elbows and arms close to your body. Keep your back straight during the lift by tightening the stomach muscles, bending at the knees, and looking up and ahead.

***STOP WORK if things feel off-normal or any safety figures fail to work or cable/parameters fail to work. Turn off the device, unplug the power or remove the battery and store the device safely back in its suitcase. Notify Radiation Protection group either through the RPG Request Help Desk Portal or calling x7277 for urgent nonemergency assistance.

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > 3 Sample Preparation

Fill a clean sample cup with the biomass sample, preferably milled to approximately 2 mm particle size. Carefully stretch the film over the opening of the sample cup to ensure a smooth, wrinkle-free surface, and secure it in place using the saw ring part. Finally, print the sample ID and label the sample cup accurately.

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > Note

Ensure that the sample cup is thoroughly cleaned prior to use. Any residual material may contaminate the sample and lead to inaccurate analytical results.

The workstation must be used when operating under the workstation account to perform XRF measurements in Room 3219. Improper setup of the workstation may result in X-ray exposure to the operator and others in the room during measurement. Never initiate a measurement without ensuring that the workstation cover is properly closed and securely locked.

<!-- image -->

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > Note

The XRF analyzer can be powered either by its internal battery or by using an AC power adapter to operate at 50 kV.

1. Acquire the XRF analyzer suitcase and the work station from the XRF cabinet in room 3219.
2. Set up the laptop and log in with user name and password written on the laptop.
3. Unlock the suitcase and remove the XRF analyzer from the suitcase and insert the battery into the XRF analyzer, which is at the bottom of the equipment. Make sure the battery is in the right direction when inserting it into the analyzer. Put back the battery cap into the XRF analyzer.
4. Connect the USB cable from the XRF to the laptop.
5. Turn on the analyzer by pressing the ON/OFF button on the right side of the analyzer, hold for 3 seconds until the screen is on.
6. Assemble the XRF analyzer into the Workstation, connect the cable from the back of the Workstation to the room electrical outlet to power on the Workstation. The Workstation will flash a red light indicating it is ON.
7. Open the Workstation cover and place the sample cup facing the XRF analyzer's Xray measurement window.
8. Close the Workstation cover and lock it in place. The lock is located outside, on the right of the Work station.

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > Note

- Ensure the cable connecting the XRF analyzer to the laptop is inserted to the top of the XRF analyzer before assembling the XRF analyzer to the Workstation. When done assembling, the operator will not be able to connect this cable. ■
- The XRF analyzer's camera, proximity sensor, and X-ray measurement window should fit properly into the rectangle gap inside the Workstation. When assembling correctly, the operator will hear a click noise indicating that the position is locked in place. After confirming, the operator can release their hands from supporting the XRF analyzer and XRF analyzer will not move. The lock is located on the back of the Workstation. □

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > 5 Vanta2 App Log in and Measurement

1. Open Vanta2 Desktop app in the laptop.
2. Select User\_Workstan from the available list and log in with code.
3. When ready, click the play button on the screen to  measure each biomass sample 3 times.
4. When measurement is completed, unlock and open the workstation cover. Wait for the app to show "Not Ready" then proceed to remove the completed sample cup and load a new sample cup.
section_path: 5 Vanta2 App Log in and Measurement

content:
p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > Safety information

While measuring, the app screen will show X-ray ON and measurement is Active. XRF analyzer's light will flash red and Work station's LED light will also flash red. When measurement is in process, DO NOT OPEN THE WORKSTATION COVER!!! If the Workstation cover is opened and unlocked but the app says 'Ready', this means the safety function does not work. STOP WORK and report!!!

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > Note

Geochem(3-beam) will take 50 seconds to complete each biomass sample. The remaining time counting is shown at the bottom left of the app screen.

<!-- image -->

Measurement in progress

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > 6 Data Export & Shutting Down

1. Go to the Menu Tray and select the Export setting.
2. Change File name if needed and click 'Browse' to select a location folder for the data.
3. Go back to the Menu Tray and select Export Today. Export data will be in the csv file.
4. When finishing measuring all samples, go to the Menu Tray and select the Logout Session.
5. The logout window will pop up. Select OK to log out.
6. Press and hold the ON/OFF button to turn off the XRF analyzer. The XRF analyzer screen will show Shutting down..
7. Disassemble the Workstation and remove the XRF analyzer from the Workstation.
8. Remove the battery from the XRF analyzer and charge it if needed. If using the plug in power directly to the wall, unplug the power.
9. Return the XRF analyzer, cable to the suitcase and the Workstation back into the XRF cabinet. Remember to lock the suitcase while in storage.
10. Store/discard the sample properly after usage.

<!-- image -->

Logout session in the Menu Tray

p1-2-x-ray-fluorescence-testing-of-biomass-hh8mb39u7 > Safety information

The field stand kit must be used under the Chamber account when the workstation is not applicable for XRF measurements; it must be properly set up to prevent any leakage of X-rays during operation. This set up doesn't require the Vanta2 desktop app and operator will access the Menu Tray directly from the XRF analyzer monitor.

1. Unlock the suitcase and acquire the XRF analyzer device and the field stand kit from the XRF cabinet.
2. Insert the battery or plug in the power directly to the wall using the adapter and cord.
3. Turn ON the XRF analyzer.
4. When the initiation stage is finished, select the User\_Chamber account from the available list and type in code to log in.
5. Install the XRF analyzer into the docking cradle to secure the XRF analyzer on a bench and carefully install the analyzer locker to the XRF analyzer's X-ray measurement window.
6. Place the sample cup properly.
7. Install the heavy cap to cover the sample cup as a shielded sample chamber.
8. When ready to measure, hold the trigger for at least 55 seconds for Geochem(3Beam). The XRF analyzer light will flash red to indicate measurement is in progress.
9. The XRF analyzer light will stop flashing red when the measurement is completed. Release your fingers from the trigger.
10. To check the result data, disassemble the heavy cap, remove the sample cup, remove the analyzer locker and the XRF analyzer from the docking cradle to gain access to the monitor screen.
11. When done using the analyzer, select Logout Session from the Menu tray and press and hold the ON/OFF button to turn off the XRF analyzer. The XRF analyzer screen will

<!-- image -->

- show Shutting down..
12. Remove the battery from the XRF analyzer and charge it if needed. If using the plug in power adapter directly to the wall, unplug the power adapter.
13. Return the XRF analyzer to the suitcase and the Vanta Field Stand kit back into the XRF cabinet. Remember to lock the suitcase while in storage.
14. Store/discard the sample properly after usage.
